script_body: Gotham's splendid “city within a city” was built in the 1930s at the height of the Depression. Thanks to the jobs it gave construction workers, it was the city's second-largest employer at the time, surpassed only by the federal Works Progress Administration. It remains a marvel of elegance and aspiration, a several-blocks-wide collection of 19 buildings that, despite their mass, create a space that is airy and light — a welcoming haven for both tourists and residents.

Directly behind the statue, a plaque marks the space where the 70-plus-foot Christmas tree is set on November 20 each year.

script_body: Adam Gopnik wrote about Times Square in The New Yorker, “No other part of New York has had such a melodramatic sensitivity to the changes in the city's history, with an image for every decade.” Think for a moment and the visions flood in: snazzy clubs and peroxide blonde chorus girls in the 1920s and '30s, sailors kissing girls at the end of World War II, the wisecracking small-time hoods of Guys and Dolls in the '50s, and the bleak urban decay of the '60s and '70s when, as Gopnik put it, “everything fell apart and Hell wafted up through the manhole covers.” Times Square is back on the upswing now, the porn shops banished and crime held mostly at bay.

script_body: Automaker Walter P. Chrysler commissioned architect William Van Alen to top them all, telling him he wanted a building “higher than the Eiffel Tower.” But the men behind the Bank of America had the same ambition, and hired Van Alen's former partner and sworn enemy, H. Craig Severance, to build the tallest building on the planet down on Wall Street. As each architect returned to the drafting board, Severance was sure he had won, completing the Bank of America building at 927 feet. Van Alen then unveiled the coup de grâce he'd been hiding in an elevator shaft — a silver spike to crown his building, making it, at 1,046 feet, an unbeatable 117 feet higher than his rival's.

script_body: There's no better introduction to New York than a visit to the Empire State Building. It's an apex of the New York skyline, both literally at 102 stories and 1,454 feet, and figuratively. From your bird's-eye perch you orient yourself geographically and see, with a clarity not possible on the ground, the miracle of Manhattan — that runt of an island that couldn't get much wider or longer, and so did what no other city before it had done and expanded to the skies, becoming a dense, pulsating city of boxy towers on a painfully narrow strip of land.

script_body: The Empire State Building opened in 1931 after just 14 months of construction, at a total cost of $25 million. It was the tallest building in the world from 1931 to 1970, when the World Trade Center took the title; it's still the 32nd tallest building on the planet. The oddly shaped spire at the top was meant to be a landing port for blimps, but high winds kept dirigibles from ever being able to anchor here.

script_body: In ancient Roman times, the entrances to great cities were framed with monumental arches meant to awe all who passed through. When Grand Central Terminal was built at the turn of the last century, its architects recognized that railroad terminals were the city's grand gateways, and filled them with the symbols of imperial Rome. On Grand Central's south facade, 10 colossal Doric fluted pillars tower over Park Avenue; above them, a massive statue of Mercury, the god of travel, spreads his arms in welcome as Hercules and Minerva, gods of strength and wisdom, lounge at his feet. The face of the clock below the sculpture is the largest piece of Tiffany glass in the world.

Massive windows throw shafts of light onto the acre-long Tennessee marble floor. One of the station's innovations was the use of electric lights, so you'll see bare bulbs sprinkled throughout the station and on the massive chandeliers that overhang the concourse. Two hundred buildings were demolished to make way for the station, which opened on February 2, 1913, bearing a price tag of $80 million.

script_body: The Morgan contains examples of the written word from the beginning of recorded time — from pictorial Mesopotamian cylinder seals of the 4th millennium B.C., to papyrus rolls from ancient Egypt, Greece, and Rome, to brilliantly colorful medieval illuminated manuscripts. Its crowning jewels are three editions of the Gutenberg Bible, the first book created using movable type. This is the only collection in the world to boast three editions; scholars come from around the globe to study them, as each is unique. Also in the collection are manuscripts by Mark Twain, Jane Austen, Charles Dickens, the Brontë sisters, Galileo, Bob Dylan, and James Joyce, one of 25 known surviving copies of the Declaration of Independence, and a First Folio of Shakespeare.

script_body: Can an observation deck be a work of art? That's the provocative question developer SL Green Realty posed when it hired artist Kenzo Digital to create an immersive experience atop its newest skyscraper. Set right on 42nd Street, Summit One has heart-of-the-action views like the Empire State Building's, with even better views of the Chrysler Building since it's just a few buildings over. Those views are amplified and fractured by mirrors covering most of this 1,750,212-square-foot space — and the floors are mirrored too. Other surprises include three fully transparent “sky boxes” jutting from the side of the building, letting brave visitors stare down 1,063 feet to the sidewalk, a room with floating mirrored orbs, and a digital screen that transposes visitors' faces onto clouds.

When you enter this handsome museum, you're loaned a whiz-bang electronic stylus and pen. Press the "X"-marked end of the tool to the wall text and you save what you're seeing to a customized website, to learn more later at home — your ticket comes with a personal URL, so you don't have to give up your email or any personal info. The other side of the gadget works as a pen, used at large electronic drafting tables throughout the museum, where what you design can be projected onto the walls around you.

script_body: The Met was founded fairly late, conceived in 1870 by a group of wealthy businessmen and artists. A decade later Calvert Vaux, one of the architects of Central Park, was brought in to create the first red-brick building on this site — you can still see that facade, now the side wall of the European Sculpture Court. A little over a decade later an expansion was needed, so famed architect Richard Morris Hunt was tapped to create the majestic neoclassical Indiana-limestone edifice you see today, awing visitors who climb its mountain of steps and walk past its redwood-height pillars.

Never a static institution, the museum and its collection have continued to grow, with the Met currently owning more than 3 million works of art spanning 5,000 years. You must choose carefully among the 18 curatorial departments and decide what interests you most. On view are masterworks from nearly all the world’s cultures—from Egyptian mummies to ancient Greek statuary to Islamic carvings to Renaissance paintings to Native American masks to 20th-century decorative arts.

Its centerpiece is the Temple of Dendur, an actual temple to the goddess Isis dating to about 15 b.c. that was saved from the rising waters of the Nile after the construction of the Aswan Dam.

poi_name: Museum of the City of New York
script_body: Thanks to a 2016 overhaul, this century-old museum, founded in 1923, finally makes good on the promise of its name. It offers a textured, dramatic look at the improbable tale of a tiny, obscure Dutch colony that blossomed — and burned, and conned, and fought — into a world capital. Start in the basement, where a 30-minute film narrated by Stanley Tucci outlines the story, then move to the ground floor, where a gallery traces Gotham's history from Native American days through the 1900s, with electronic panels profiling New Yorkers from Alexander Hamilton to a murdered prostitute.

source_passage: Thanks to a 2016 overhaul, this century-old museum (founded in 1923) is finally making good on the promise of its name. Today, it offers visitors a textured, dramatic, suavely interactive look at the improbable tale of a tiny, obscure Dutch colony that blossomed—and burned, and conned, and fought—into a world capital. Start your visit in the basement, where an absorbing 30-minute film (narrated by Stanley Tucci) outlines the story. Next stop should be ground floor, where one gallery traces Gotham’s history from Native American days through the 1900s, displaying artifacts of all sorts, accompanied by electronic panels offering biographies of New Yorkers both well-known and obscure—everyone from Alexander Hamilton to a murdered prostitute—that illuminate different strands of the story.

Bauhaus furniture, and its collection of drawings by Teutonic masters such as Dix, Schiele, and Breuer. Because some of those drawings are a bit racy, children 11 and under are not admitted.

script_body: New York is the city of the rectangle and the sharp right angle — our streets a grid, our buildings boxy and regular — until you get to the Guggenheim. Frank Lloyd Wright's delirious spiral of a museum sits among the towers of Fifth Avenue like a steroidal peacock among guinea hens. Critic Herbert Muschamp described it best: "What else but a building brought back from a dream would be windowless, have walls and floors that tilt and twist, begin on the top floor, and spiral in towards the center like an enigma?" Visiting this 1959 masterpiece and trudging up the ramps of its curving halls turns the standard museum experience into a profound journey — and sometimes a battle against vertigo.

script_body: Early critics dismissed the Guggenheim — Newsweek's insipid review was headlined "Museum or Cupcake?" — yet Frommer's argues even the most jaded visitor today feels the power of the place, the symbolic weight of infinite circle upon circle. And to answer the question nobody ever voices aloud: no, there have been no suicide jumps from over the low-slung rails, nor has anyone ever accidentally fallen to their death.

script_body: Since 1869 this institution has been both the country's preeminent private scientific research facility and its top museum for paleontology, zoology, anthropology, and now astronomy — and the flow between its research and curatorial sides keeps it fiercely vital. A few years ago scientists concluded that dinosaurs had not dragged their tails as long thought but waved them in the air as they walked. The curators responded by painstakingly dismantling the famed dino skeletons and reassembling them with tails erect, then placed one skeleton atop a section of a Texas riverbed where they had found fossilized dino footprints with no tail-dragging marks — a peephole into how scientific theories emerge.

The curators responded, painstakingly dismantling the museum’s famed dino skeletons and reassembling them with tails erect. Then, in a brilliant stroke, they placed one skeleton atop a section of a Texas riverbed where they had found fossilized dino footprints (sans tail-dragging marks), giving museumgoers a peephole into how scientific theories emerge.

script_body: In 2023 the $431-million Richard Gilder Center for Science, Education and Innovation opened, transforming the museum-going experience. Its new 230,000-square-foot structure houses 12% of the museum's collections, including an insectarium, a permanent butterfly vivarium, open storage exhibits, and a 360-degree Invisible Worlds Theater about the networks that underlie all life. Be sure to enter through this new center: the dazzling lobby mimics curving Southwestern American canyons, a sinuous look created by spraying structural concrete directly onto rebar.

poi_name: Cathedral of St. John the Divine
script_body: Three odd facts make this a fascinating building. First: the largest cathedral in the world isn't St. Peter's in Rome — which is technically not a cathedral but a basilica — it's St. John the Divine in upper Manhattan. Second: despite the popish name, it isn't Catholic, it's Episcopalian. Third: though construction began in 1892, the building is still not complete, and many estimate it will take another 100 years to finish. The 121,000-square-foot structure blends Romanesque and Gothic elements, thanks to the varying tastes of the architects who worked on it over the past century. Most striking, it's being built without steel, in the classic Gothic manner — to that end, in 1979 a master stonecutter was brought from England to train Harlem youths in the art of traditional stonecutting. Much work remains, but what's in place is quite beautiful, especially the Rose Window in the apse, the largest in North America.

script_body: When you're NYC's oldest museum, founded in 1804, your attic gets mighty full. In past years that fourth-floor "attic" felt like a treasure hunt, its open storage units overflowing with telling artifacts — a Tiffany lamp here, a pair of historic pistols there, the plaster model head sculptor Daniel Chester French created for Washington's Lincoln Memorial in another corner. Then in 2017 the curators tidied up, replacing the open storage with three not-so-successful permanent galleries: a runway of too-many Tiffany lamps, a room of themed glass cases on facets of city life like "Childhood," "Fire," and "Collecting," and a center for women's history.

script_body: An offshoot of the Metropolitan Museum, the Cloisters is the only museum in the United States devoted wholly to medieval art, and it shows its masterworks in a setting that seems airlifted intact from some remote corner of the Pyrenees, or from a castle-lined town in Bavaria. Opened in 1934, the museum was in fact built in the United States, but 30% of its architectural elements — columns, pedestals, naves, doorframes, exquisite stained-glass windows — were salvaged from medieval European structures. It's a stunning mirage: even the land across the river was bought by patron John D. Rockefeller to thwart development and ensure the Cloisters' views would forever have a medieval face. At its heart are four cloisters, garden areas centered with a fountain and surrounded by covered walkways of the type seen in every monastery and abbey in Europe.

script_body: Pay special attention to the Unicorn Tapestries, one of only two full sets with a unicorn theme in the world — the other is in Paris. These richly detailed tapestries can be read on many levels: many scholars see the unicorn as a symbol of Christ, and the hunt to slay it as evocative of the Passion; others read the work as a metaphor for courtly love, with the hunt as courtship and the final tapestry — the unicorn trapped inside a wedding-ring-like fence — symbolizing marriage. Despite this captivity, the unicorn does look happy. They are an evocative slice of a past when nobles only hunted in packs of six, and unicorns were thought to be real — hence the long narwhal tooth in this room, which medieval people believed came from a unicorn.

script_body: The other must-see items are kept in the climate-controlled Campin Room — bring a sweater. There you'll find Robert de Campin's breakthrough Merode altarpiece, from around 1425, which placed the Annunciation — the moment an angel tells the Virgin Mary she will bear the child of God — in a secular setting rather than a church. It's also dramatic for its use of Jewish objects, including a prayer shawl and a vase with Hebrew-looking lettering, to establish Mary's background. Nearby is the so-called Cloisters Cross, one of only three known ivory crosses preserved from the 12th century — and the most complex, with over 90 figures and inscriptions painstakingly carved into the walrus-tusk ivory.

script_body: The Brooklyn Museum's Egyptian Collection, while not as extensive as the Met's, arguably has more masterpieces. When an ancient Egyptian piece comes up at auction, dealers often ask, 'Is it Brooklyn quality?' — the museum's collection being the benchmark for this sort of artifact. Among its wonders are a tiny 5,000-year-old, pre-dynastic terra cotta sculpture of a woman, nicknamed 'Birdwoman' for her beaklike face, and the Cartonnage of Nespanetjerenpere, a mummy case whose colors are electrically bright and unfaded.

source_passage: Its Egyptian Collection, while not as extensive as the Met's, arguably has more masterpieces. (When an ancient Egyptian piece comes up at auction, dealers often ask, “Is it Brooklyn quality?”—the Brooklyn Museum's collection being the benchmark for this sort of artifact.) Among the collection's many wonders are a tiny 5,000-year-old, pre-dynastic terra cotta sculpture of a woman, which curators have nicknamed “Birdwoman” for her beaklike face, one of very few intact sculptures from this long-ago era. The Cartonnage of Nespanetjerenpere is another highlight, a mummy case that looks like it was swiped from the set of Revenge of the Mummy, its colors electrically bright and unfaded.

The oral histories of the women who worked here during the war, preserved at the on-site museum, are especially moving.

script_body: The Yard's importance to America began far earlier, during the American Revolution, when the British docked their infamous prison ships here. Conditions aboard them were so atrocious that more than 11,500 Americans perished — more than the combined U.S. casualties in all the battles of the Revolution. Most of their bodies were simply dumped overboard into the water, making these waters the largest Revolutionary graveyard in the States.

Its sea lions and most of the other aquatic critters surfed the storm unhurt, but the buildings were heavily damaged, new construction was put on hold, and visitors could only see 40% of the facilities. That changed in the summer of 2018, when the whiz-bang Ocean Wonders center opened.

script_body: The no. 7 train — which originates at Times Square and snakes mostly above ground through the heart of ethnic Queens — is popularly known as the International Express. Built by immigrants in the early 1900s, the no. 7 IRT brought those same immigrants to homes on the outer fringes of the city, and that tradition has continued as newcomers settle close by its elevated tracks. Get off in Sunnyside for Romanian groceries, in Jackson Heights for Indian saris and Sikh turbans, or ride to Flushing, where Queens's Chinatown is bigger than Manhattan's. In 1999 it was nominated as a National Millennium Trail and chosen to represent the American immigrant experience.

source_passage: The no. 7 train—which originates in Manhattan at Times Square, makes three stops in that borough, and then snakes, mostly above ground, through the heart of ethnic Queens—is also popularly known as the International Express. Built by immigrants in the early 1900s, the no. 7 IRT (Interborough Rapid Transit) brought those same immigrants to homes on the outer fringes of New York City. That tradition has continued as immigrants from around the world have settled close by the no. 7's elevated tracks. Get off in Sunnyside and see Romanian grocery stores and restaurants; a few stops farther in Jackson Heights, you'll see Indians in saris and Sikhs in turbans; go all the way to Flushing and you'll think you are in Chinatown. (You are—Queen's Chinatown is bigger than Manhattan's.) In 1999, the Queens Council on the Arts nominated the International Express for designation as a National Millennium Trail, and that resulted in its selection as representative of the American immigrant experience by the White House Millennium Council, the United States Department of Transportation, and the Rails-to-Trails Conservancy.

script_body: Manhattan’s 843-acre green oasis feels like nature, but very little here is natural. Every tree, every shrub, every lake, and most of the rolling hills were designed, planted, or blasted into existence by landscape architects Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux back in the 1850s. The two took a two-and-a-half-mile tract of swampland, farms, and suburban towns and created an Arcadia that bore no resemblance to what came before. Underneath the park, 95 miles of drainage pipes were laid to fill and periodically empty the four man-made lakes; at ground level the site was transformed with six million bricks, 65,000 cubic tons of gravel, 26,000 trees, and 250,000 shrubs. Even the dirt was imported — the natural topsoil was so poor that 500,000 cubic feet of it was shipped in from New Jersey. As Olmsted wrote, “Every foot of the park, every tree and bush, every arch, roadway and walk, has been fixed where it is with a purpose.”

Every tree, every shrub, every lake, and most of the rolling hills were designed, planted, or blasted into existence by landscape architects Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux back in the 1850s, and their efforts still shape our experiences today. These two geniuses took a 21⁄2-mile tract of swampland, farms, and suburban towns and created an Arcadia that had no resemblance whatever to what had come before. Underneath the park, 95 miles of drainage pipes were installed, many to fill and periodically empty the four lakes that were created; at ground level the site was transformed using six million bricks, 65,000 cubic tons of gravel, 26,000 trees, and 250,000 shrubs. Even the dirt was imported; the natural topsoil was so poor that 500,000 cubic feet of topsoil was shipped in from New Jersey. As Olmsted once wrote, “Every foot of the park, every tree and bush, every arch, roadway and walk, has been fixed where it is with a purpose.”

script_body: The park’s purpose was nothing less than the health of the city — a place where New Yorkers could blow off steam and escape the stresses of urban life. Olmsted wanted more: a park that would be a bridge between classes. “There need to be places and time for re-unions,” he wrote, “[where] the rich and the poor, the cultivated and the self-made, shall be attracted together and encouraged to assimilate.” It didn’t happen at first — the park was too far from the homes of poor New Yorkers for them to visit — but that ideal was realized once the city itself wrapped around the park, finally making it a true central park.

source_passage: And what was that purpose? No less than the health of the city. Those who rallied for its creation felt that it was crucial to create a place where New Yorkers could blow off steam and get away from the stresses of urban life. Moreover, Olmsted wanted to create a park that would be a bridge between classes. “There need to be places and time for re-unions,” Olmsted wrote, “[where] the rich and the poor, the cultivated and the self-made, shall be attracted together and encouraged to assimilate.” Though that didn’t happen when the park was first finished—it was too far from the homes of poor New Yorkers for them to visit it—that ideal was realized when the city itself began to wrap around the park, making it finally a true central park.

script_body: As you stroll, you’ll cross three deliberately different kinds of landscape. There are pastoral vistas like the Sheep Meadow, meant to evoke a cultivated countryside; primitive portions where dense forestation shuts out any view of the city; and promenade zones, once used by the city’s aristocracy as an extension of their parlors — a place to strut and be seen. There’s no right way to see the park; you can ignore any highlight list and simply wander its curving paths for hidden nooks and surprise vistas.

I’ve created a brief list of highlights that includes all three, but feel free to ignore the list altogether and just wander the curving paths of the park, exploring its hidden nooks, surprise vistas, ball fields, and playgrounds. script_body: This turreted castle is Olmsted and Vaux’s “folly” — a fantasy building — and it sits atop the second-highest elevation in the park. Inside is a nature observatory with good rainy-day activities for children. From Belvedere you also look down on the Great Lawn, which has gone through a number of incarnations: first a reservoir, then in the 1930s “Hooverville,” the shantytown where hundreds of homeless families lived out the Depression. Today it’s laid out in ballfields and often used as a concert space — Simon and Garfunkel famously reunited here in the 1980s in a widely televised concert.

script_body: This handsome obelisk was a gift to the United States from Egypt in 1881, in recognition of the help this country gave in building the Suez Canal. Transporting the 200-ton pillar took 38 days by ship from Alexandria to New York — and then another 144 days just to haul it from the Hudson River into Central Park. It originally stood at the Temple of the Sun in Heliopolis, believed to have been erected in 1600 b.c.; the Romans moved it in the 12th century to the front of a temple built by Cleopatra, which is how it got its name. A plaque at the base translates the hieroglyphics.

Transporting the 200-ton pillar took 38 days from Alexandria to New York by ship, and then another 144 just to get it from the Hudson River to Central Park. It originally stood at the Temple of the Sun in Heliopolis, and is believed to have been erected in 1600 b.c. The Romans moved it in the 12th century to the front of a temple built by Cleopatra, hence the name. A plaque at the base translates the hieroglyphics.

script_body: At the southernmost tip of Manhattan, Battery Park has been growing kudzu-like for decades — it’s now a string of eclectic park spaces hugging the waterfront from just above the original Battery Park, where the Statue of Liberty ferry terminal sits, all the way up to Chambers Street, 21 acres in all. At the downtown-most end are stirring war monuments and the Seaglass Carousel, which dips and swoops riders around on massive plexiglass fish. Walking uptown you’ll find expansive lawns, a riverside promenade, terrific playgrounds, and a yacht marina.

script_body: Who knew “adaptive reuse” could be this sexy? Domino Park sits on riverside property once owned by the Domino Sugar Refinery. In adapting the land, designer Lisa Switkin — of the firm behind the High Line — protected the landmarked refinery, making the hulking factory a spooky centerpiece, and reused other industrial artifacts to wonderful effect. That includes a gantry, a massive platform holding two cranes, painted the same turquoise that once lined the refinery’s walls; it’s now an elevated walkway with spectacular Manhattan views. In front of it sits a playground built to look like a mini-refinery, a volleyball court flanked by old syrup tanks, and a grove of metal corkscrews once used to stir syrup.

script_body: Situated a half-mile south of Manhattan, the 172-acre Governors Island was for many years a Coast Guard installation. Before that it was an army post for nearly 200 years and played a part in the Revolutionary War. In April 2010, New York City took it over. Because it had been a military base for so long, few New Yorkers — much less tourists — had ever visited. That has changed: much of the island is now a public park, with 22 acres designated a national monument centered around two 1812-era fortresses. In 2016, new parkland crowned by four man-made hills opened, giving visitors even more stellar views of Manhattan.

script_body: For years a secret, untamed garden hovered above the cityscape of Chelsea and Hell’s Kitchen. Formed from wild grass, flower, and weed seeds that randomly blew onto the tracks of a mile-and-a-half abandoned elevated railway, it became a hidden-in-plain-sight oasis for those New Yorkers brave and limber enough to scale the trestles. When the city began planning to tear down the historic rail structure — constructed 1929 to 1934 — a movement was born to save it and turn it into a grand public promenade with easy access from the street. Opened in 2009, it’s beautifully landscaped, in many places with the very “weeds” that once grew there, replanted where they wouldn’t crowd out the rest.

script_body: Gotham’s newest park seems to float like a watery mirage in the Hudson River. The engineering and architecture by Thomas Featherwick — the designer of Vessel — is stupendous: a set of 132 concrete “tulips,” all of differing heights, emerge from the water and join to form the base of the isle. On top of that Seuss-like structure are hills, amphitheaters, and eateries linked by winding paths and boulder scrambles. Landscaper Signe Nielson spared no expense, reportedly spending $5 million to cover the island with some 35 species of trees and 270 varieties of perennials, grasses, and bulbs, many chosen to attract bees and birds. It’s a gift to the city from media mogul Barry Diller, who spent $260 million on its construction.

script_body: Also known as Jeffrey’s Hook Lighthouse, this historic beauty sits under the George Washington Bridge in Fort Washington Park, and it inspired the 1942 children’s classic The Little Red Lighthouse and the Great Gray Bridge by Hildegarde Swift and Lynd Ward. Built in New Jersey in 1880, it was reconstructed and moved to this spot in 1921 and stayed operational until 1947. It was slated for removal in 1951, but a public outcry over its popularity saved it; it’s now a New York City landmark and on the National Register of Historic Places.

Built in New Jersey in 1880 and reconstructed and moved to its current spot in 1921, it was operational until 1947. The lighthouse was to be removed in 1951, but because of its popularity there was a public outcry and it was saved. It’s now a New York City landmark and on the National Register of Historic Places.

script_body: Designed by Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux after their success with Central Park, this 562-acre expanse of woodland, meadows, and ponds is considered by many to be their masterpiece and the pièce de résistance of Brooklyn. The best approach is from Grand Army Plaza, presided over by the monumental Soldiers’ and Sailors’ Memorial Arch of 1892, honoring Union veterans. For the finest view of the lush landscape, follow the path to Meadowport Arch and on through to the Long Meadow, taking the loop around it — about an hour’s walk.

script_body: Prospect Park is studded with historic buildings. There’s the 1857 Italianate mansion Litchfield Villa on Prospect Park West; a 1906 Beaux Arts boathouse; a 1912 carousel whose white wooden horses were salvaged from a famous Coney Island merry-go-round; and the Lefferts Homestead Children’s Historic House Museum, a 1783 Dutch farmhouse with period furniture and kid-focused exhibits.

script_body: Another masterwork by Olmsted and Vaux, Riverside Park has always had one advantage over Central Park: glorious river views, which its garden-laced promenades make the most of. Among its monuments is Grant’s Tomb at 122nd Street, the largest mausoleum in the United States at 8,100 square feet. And the answer to that old riddle — who’s buried in Grant’s tomb? — is: no one. Ulysses S. Grant and his wife aren’t buried at all; their sarcophagi lie above ground.

script_body: This is the city’s funkiest green space, and it’s seen its share of political protest. In 1988, a standoff between the police and the homeless people living here culminated in five days of rioting and charges of police brutality. Incorporated as a park in 1878, Tompkins Square once had a band shell where an early version of the Grateful Dead made their East Coast debut, though that has since been torn down.

script_body: Union Square Park’s tradition of political activism goes back to the very first Labor Day Parade in 1882, which ended right here. Ever since, it’s been soapbox central — a place where orators come daily to blast whatever administration is in power and weigh in on the big topics of the day. A statue of Gandhi, a gift of the Indian people, calmly watches over the proceedings, a fresh wreath of flowers always draped about his neck.

script_body: This park is nothing if not tuneful: it has long been a gathering place for amateur musicians, who lug their instruments here for impromptu concerts each weekend and many fine-weather weeknights. The round fountain in the center serves as a stage for a dozen or so regular comedians, acrobats, and dancers good enough to draw crowds of a hundred people or more. And on the park’s southwest corner, intense chess matches run from noon to sundown — the regulars are real sharks.

script_body: Lincoln Center is a giant complex of theaters on the west side of Manhattan, flanking Columbus Avenue between 62nd and 65th streets. It hosts everything from major symphonic premieres to the Big Apple Circus, but it's most famous for its presentation of classic works of music, dance, opera, film, and theater. Toward that end it houses a number of permanent companies and plays host to the world's leading performing arts organizations.

script_body: Behind these walls live some of the most storied names in American performing arts. The resident companies include the Chamber Music Society of Lincoln Center, the Film Society of Lincoln Center, and Lincoln Center Theater — the last of which houses both a well-respected Broadway theater and an off-Broadway theater. Among the center's other residents are the Metropolitan Opera, the New York City Ballet, the Juilliard School, the New York Philharmonic, and the American Ballet Theatre.

script_body: Here's the lovely little secret about this house: the cheap seats get the best sound. Sit in the pricey orchestra section and you may have trouble making out the words, but buy a “family circle” seat way up high and the voices will float up to you in all their crystalline clarity. One warning, though — don't show up late. The Met does not seat latecomers; arrive after the curtain and you'll watch the first act on a video screen in the basement.

script_body: The blockbuster modern dance shows tend to play the Joyce, and it's not hard to see why — it's simply the best space in the city to see dance, with not a bad seat in the house. In this renovated, Art Deco-era movie theater, the audience sits slightly above the dancers, so you won't be seeing just the feet or just the bodies; you'll get the whole picture. Pilobolus has played here, as well as the Limon Dance Company, Trisha Brown, and Savion Glover.

script_body: The New York City Ballet was founded by Lincoln Kirstein and the twentieth century's greatest ballet choreographer, George Balanchine. It is for Balanchine's work that you still attend performances here at the David H. Koch Theater; his choreography is the staple, and it remains as diamond-sharp, elegant, and moving as when it was first performed as many as fifty years ago. Balanchine's version of The Nutcracker is a holiday classic and one of the most difficult tickets to get each Christmas season.

script_body: Bartholdi spent almost 20 years turning his dream into reality: a hollow copper colossus mounted in New York Harbor. The project was hindered by serious financial problems but helped by the fund-raising efforts of newspaper publisher Joseph Pulitzer, and by poet Emma Lazarus, whose ode to Lady Liberty was part of a campaign for the pedestal, designed by American architect Richard Morris Hunt. Bartholdi's work was also delayed by structural challenges, a problem resolved by the metal-framework mastery of railway engineer Gustave Eiffel, yes, of the famous tower. Completed in France in 1884, the statue was shipped to NYC as 350 pieces packed into 214 crates and reassembled over four months on the US-made granite pedestal.

source_passage: Bartholdi spent almost 20 years turning his dream - to create the hollow copper colossus and mount it in New York Harbor - into reality. Along the way the project was hindered by serious financial problems but helped in part by the fund-raising efforts of newspaper publisher Joseph Pulitzer. Lending a further hand was poet Emma Lazarus, whose ode to Lady Liberty was part of a fund-raising campaign for the statue's pedestal, designed by American architect Richard Morris Hunt. Bartholdi's work on the statue was also delayed by structural challenges - a problem resolved by the metal-framework mastery of railway engineer Gustave Eiffel (yes, of the famous tower). The work of art was finally completed in France in 1884, a bit behind schedule for the centennial. It was shipped to NYC as 350 pieces packed into 214 crates, reassembled over a span of four months and placed on the US-made granite pedestal.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions. Statue remains on its granite pedestal in New York Harbor; copper colossus intact.

script_body: The most famous port of entry in the world, and a physical symbol of the American immigrant story, Ellis Island is now a National Monument. Operating only from 1892 to 1924, it nonetheless processed some 12 million new arrivals. An estimated 40% of Americans today descend from those millions, making this island central to the story of modern America.

script_body: Architects Edward Lippincott Tilton and William A Boring won the contract after the original wooden building burnt down in 1897, and having attended the Ecole des Beaux-Arts in Paris, they opted for a beaux-arts aesthetic. The Main Building evokes a grand train station, with majestic triple-arched entrances, decorative Flemish bond brickwork, and granite cornerstones and belvederes. Inside, the vast Registry Room takes the breath away. Its original plaster ceiling was severely damaged by an explosion of munition barges at nearby Black Tom Wharf, a blessing in disguise, as the rebuilt version was adorned with striking herringbone-patterned tiles by Rafael Guastavino.

script_body: Ellis Island's very first immigrant was 17-year-old Anna 'Annie' Moore. After a 12-day journey in steerage from County Cork, Ireland, Annie arrived on January 1, 1892, accompanied by her brothers Phillip and Anthony; the three were headed to America to join their parents, who had migrated to New York City four years earlier. She later married German immigrant Joseph Augustus Schayer and gave birth to at least 11 children, only five of whom survived. Annie died on December 6, 1924, and was laid to rest at Calvary Cemetery, Queens.

script_body: Surrounded by a plaza planted with more than 400 white oak trees, the 9/11 Memorial's reflecting pools occupy the footprints of the ill-fated Twin Towers. From their rim, a cascade of water pours 30ft down toward a central void. The flow is richly symbolic, beginning as thousands of smaller streams, merging into a massive torrent of collective confusion, and ending with a slow journey toward an abyss. Bronze panels frame the pools, inscribed with the names of those who died in the attacks of September 11, 2001, and in the World Trade Center car bombing on February 26, 1993. Designed by Michael Arad and Peter Walker, the pools are titled Reflecting Absence.

script_body: The museum's glass entrance pavilion eerily evokes a toppled tower. On the escalator descent to the subterranean lobby, visitors stand in the shadow of two steel tridents, originally embedded in the bedrock at the base of the North Tower. Each weighing 50 tons, they once provided the structural support that allowed the towers to soar over 1360ft into the sky, and they remained standing in the subsequent sea of rubble, becoming immediate symbols of resilience. Among more than 10,300 objects in the collection are the Vesey Street Stairs, dubbed the Survivors' Staircase, which allowed hundreds of workers to flee the WTC site on the morning of 9/11.

script_body: At the bottom of the Survivors' Staircase is the moving In Memoriam gallery, its walls lined with photographs and names of those who perished. Among the personal effects on display is a dust-covered wallet belonging to Robert Joseph Gschaar, an insurance underwriter who worked on level 92 of the South Tower. The wallet's contents include a photograph of his wife, Myrta, and a $2 bill: when he proposed, Gschaar gave her a $2 bill as a symbol of their second chance at happiness, theirs being a second marriage for both, and he kept another with him.

script_body: Around the corner from the In Memoriam gallery is the NYC Fire Department's Engine Company 21, one of the largest artifacts on display, its burnt-out cab a testament to the inferno faced by those at the scene. It stands at the entrance to the main historical exhibition, divided into Events of the Day, Before 9/11 and After 9/11. The exhibition spills into the monumental Foundation Hall, flanked by a massive section of the original slurry wall, built to hold back the waters of the Hudson River during the towers' construction. The hall is also home to the last steel column removed during the cleanup, adorned with messages and mementos of recovery workers, first responders and loved ones.

script_body: Leaping from the northwestern corner of the World Trade Center site, the 104-floor tower is architect David M Childs' redesign of Daniel Libeskind's original 2002 concept. The loftiest building in America and currently the tallest in the Western Hemisphere, this tapered giant soars with chamfered edges, forming a series of isosceles triangles that, seen from the base, reach to infinity. Crowning the structure is a 408ft cable-stayed spire, co-designed by sculptor Kenneth Snelson, which brings the building's total height to 1776ft, a symbolic reference to the year of American independence. The tower's footprint equals those of the original Twin Towers, and its observation decks match the heights of those in the old complex.

script_body: The One World Observatory experience begins at the ground-floor Global Welcome Center, where an electronic world map highlights the homelands of the building's visitors, with data relayed from ticket scans. After a Voices exhibition on 144 video screens, you step inside one of five Sky Pod elevators, among the fastest in the world. script_body: Originally named 'Nut Island,' or Paggank, by the indigenous Lenape people, the island was renamed first by the Dutch and then dubbed Governors Island when it became a military installation. Besides serving as a fort in the Revolutionary War, the Union Army's central recruiting station during the Civil War, and the take-off point for Wilbur Wright's famous 1909 flight around the Statue of Liberty, Governors Island is where the 1988 Reagan-Gorbachev summit signaled the beginning of the end of the Cold War. You can visit the spot where that summit took place at the Admiral's House, a grand, colonnaded military residence completed in 1843.

script_body: The most rewarding experience for Chinatown visitors is to access this wild and wonderful world through their taste buds. More than any other area of Manhattan, Chinatown's menus sport wonderfully low prices, uninflated by ambience, hype or reputation. But more than cheap eats, the neighborhood is rife with family recipes passed across generations and continents. Food displays and preparation remain unchanged and untempered by American norms; it's not unusual to walk by storefronts sporting a tangled array of lacquered animals — chickens, rabbit and duck, in particular — ready to be chopped up and served at a family banquet. Steaming street stalls clang down the sidewalk serving pork buns and other finger-friendly food.

script_body: When New York City's Chinatown was founded in the mid-19th century, it was immigrants from Guangdong — Canton Province — that built it. Many of the traditional shops hawking pork buns, and restaurants serving dim sum, are grounded in Cantonese culture. After the Vietnam War came Chinese groups from Vietnam, then the late 20th century brought a wave of Fujianese that caused tensions with the original community. Since then, Chinatown has become a hot pot of different Asian cultures, from Burmese to Filipino. Even Latin American flavor is creeping in down Canal St.

script_body: Traditionally Canal St has been Chinatown's spine, but the relentless force of gentrification is coming and the first sure signs can be seen here. You'll still see roasted ducks and pigs hanging by their skinny necks in windows, but it's also where you'll find persistent street vendors pushing knock-off Prada bags, and hipster design markets catering to an altogether different crowd. To find the true heart of Chinatown, find your way into the side streets: Mott and Mulberry are particularly evocative hunting grounds for treasures from the Far East. You'll pass stinky seafood stalls hawking slippery fish; mysterious herb shops peddling a witch's cauldron of roots and potions; storefront bakeries with steamy windows and 80¢ pork buns; and produce markets piled high with fresh lychees, bok choy and Asian pears.

script_body: Built in 1832 and purchased by merchant magnate Seabury Tredwell three years later, this redbrick mansion is the most authentic Federal-style house in town — one of about 300 such houses that survive. An antiquarian's dream, the Merchant's House is as much about the city's mercantile past as it is a showcase of high-end domestic furnishings from the 19th century. Everything in the house is testament to what money could buy, from the mahogany pocket doors, bronze gasoliers and marble mantelpieces, to the elegant parlor chairs, attributed to noted furniture designer Duncan Phyfe. Even the elaborate system of multilevel call bells for the servants works to this day.

script_body: The 'Hard Times' tour, one of the most popular, visits apartments from two periods — the 1870s and the 1930s. There you'll see the squalid conditions tenants faced: in the early days there was a wretched communal outhouse and no electricity or running water. Recorded testimony from a surviving member of the Baldizzi family, who lived here during the Depression, makes it easier to relate to what you see. Other tours focus on Irish immigrants and the harsh discrimination they faced, sweatshop workers and 'shop life,' with a tour through a recreated 1870s German beer hall.

There you'll see the squalid conditions tenants faced – in the early days there was a wretched communal outhouse and no electricity or running water – and what life was like for the families who lived there. Recorded testimony from a surviving member of the Baldizzi family, who lived here during the Depression, makes it easier to relate to what you see. script_body: A great way to understand the immigrant experience is on a walking tour around the neighborhood. These tours, ranging from 90 minutes to two hours, explore a variety of topics. 'Foods of the Lower East Side' looks at the ways traditional foods have shaped American cuisine; 'Outside the Home' and 'Building on the Lower East Side' look at life beyond the apartment — where immigrants stored and lost their life savings, the churches and synagogues so integral to community life, and the meeting halls where poorly paid workers gathered to fight for better conditions.

script_body: The New Museum's building is the brainchild of Japanese firm SANAA — a partnership between Kazuyo Sejima and Ryue Nishizawa. In 2010, SANAA won the coveted Pritzker Prize (think the Oscars of architecture) for its contributions to the world of design. Their trademark vanishing facades are known worldwide for abiding by a strict adherence to a form-follows-function design aesthetic, sometimes taking the land plot's footprint into the overall shape of the structure. The box-atop-box scheme provides a striking counterpoint to the clusters of crimson brick and iron fire escapes outside, while alluding to the geometric exhibition chasms within.

The institution gave gallery space to artists Keith Haring, Jeff Koons, Joan Jonas, Mary Kelly, and Andres Serrano at the beginning of their careers, and continues to show contemporary heavy-hitters. The city's sole museum dedicated to contemporary art has brought a steady menu of edgy works in new forms.

script_body: As you walk St Marks Place, keep an eye out for the tile-encrusted street poles of the Mosaic Trail. In the mid-1980s, a local Vietnam vet named Jim Power began decorating lampposts with bits of tile, mirror, ceramics, beads and coins as a way to deal with his PTSD and imbue the streets with colorful — and often political — art. Many of them portray local East Village landmarks or figures, such as 'CBGB,' 'Patti Smith' and 'PDT (Please Don't Tell).'

script_body: The 10.5-acre Tompkins Square Park honors Daniel Tompkins, who served as governor of New York from 1807 to 1817, and as the nation's vice president after that, under James Monroe. Dating from 1879, the park is like a friendly town square for locals, who gather for chess at concrete tables, picnics on the lawn, and spontaneous guitar or drum jams on various grassy knolls. It also has basketball courts, a fun-to-watch dog run, a mini public swimming pool for kids, and frequent summer concerts.

script_body: In the 1980s the park was a dirty, needle-strewn homeless encampment, unusable for folks wanting a place to stroll or picnic. A contentious turning point came when police razed the band shell and evicted more than 100 squatters living in a tent city in 1988 — and again in 1991. That first eviction turned violent: the Tompkins Square Riot ushered in the first wave of yuppies in the dog run, fashionistas lolling on the grass, and undercover narcotics agents trying to pass as druggie punk kids.

script_body: In the early 1900s the western area around the Meatpacking District and Chelsea was the largest industrial section of Manhattan. Street-level freight trains caused so much disruption and death that Tenth Ave earned the nickname 'Death Ave' for rail accidents that claimed over 500 lives. The answer was to lift the tracks: the 'West Side Elevated Line' moved its first train in 1933. The project drained over $150 million — around $2 billion in today's money — and took roughly five years to complete.

Section 1 starts at Gansevoort St and runs parallel to Tenth Ave up to W 20th St, filled with sitting space from giant chaises longues to bleacher-like benches. Two years later Section 2 added another 10 blocks of greenified tracks. In 2014 the third section was completed, from 30th up to 34th St, looping around the West Side Rail Yards in a U-like fashion.

script_body: The iconic Stanford White Arch, known colloquially as the Washington Square Arch, dominates the park with 72ft of beaming white Dover marble. It was originally designed in wood to celebrate the centennial of George Washington's inauguration in 1889; the design proved so popular that it was replaced in stone six years later and adorned with statues of the general in war and peace. In 1917 the artist Marcel Duchamp famously climbed to the top of the arch by its internal stairway and declared the park the 'Free and Independent Republic of Washington Square.'

script_body: As its maritime industry dwindled, New York had to devise a future for the bristling ranks of piers left behind. script_body: Opened in 1831, Union Square quickly became the central gathering place for those who lived in the mansions nearby. Concert halls and artist societies enhanced the cultured atmosphere, and high-end shopping proliferated along Broadway, which was dubbed 'Ladies' Mile.' When the Civil War broke out, the vast public space was center stage for protesters of all sorts, from union workers to political activists. By the height of WWI, the area had fallen largely into disuse, allowing politically and socially driven organizations like the American Civil Liberties Union, the Communist and Socialist Parties, and the Ladies' Garment Workers Union to move in. Many decades later, the square remains a popular site for political and social protests.

Concert halls and artist societies further enhanced the cultured atmosphere, and high-end shopping quickly proliferated along Broadway, which was dubbed 'Ladies' Mile.' When the Civil War broke out, the vast public space (large by New York standards, of course) was center stage for protesters of all sorts, from union workers to political activists. By the height of WWI, the area had fallen largely into disuse, allowing politically and socially driven organizations like the American Civil Liberties Union, the Communist and Socialist Parties, and the Ladies' Garment Workers Union to move in. Many decades later, the square remains a popular site for political and social protests, as well as one of NYC's best regular farmers markets.

Faithful narrative, no factual error.

script_body: On the southeastern side of the square is a massive art installation that either earns confused stares or simply gets overlooked by passersby. Metronome is a symbolic representation of the passage of time with two parts: a digital clock with a puzzling display of numbers, and a wand-like apparatus with smoke puffing out of concentric rings. The 14 numbers must be split into two groups of seven: the seven from the left tell the current time — hour, minute, second, tenth-of-a-second — and the seven from the right are meant to be read in reverse order; they represent the remaining amount of time in the day.

We'll let you ponder the latter while we give you the skinny on what exactly the winking orange digits denote: the 14 numbers must be split into two groups of seven: the seven from the left tell the current time (hour, minute, second, tenth-of-a-second) and the seven from the right are meant to be read in reverse order; they represent the remaining amount of time in the day.

script_body: Manhattan's early Dutch settlers named the area now known as Gramercy 'Krom Moerasje' — meaning Little Crooked Swamp. The swamp would meet its end in 1831, when lawyer and public official Samuel Ruggles purchased the land, had the swamp drained, and carved the territory into 108 lots. Forty-two of these were set aside for an English-style private park, to be held in perpetuity by the residents of its surrounding 66 lots.

script_body: For several decades, the dream here was a sordid one. The economic crash of the early 1970s led to a mass exodus of corporations from Times Square — billboard niches went dark, stores shut, and once-grand hotels were converted into single-room occupancy dives. While the adjoining Theater District survived, its respectable playhouses shared the streets with porn cinemas and strip clubs. That changed under tough-talking former mayor Rudolph Giuliani, who in the 1990s boosted police numbers and lured in a wave of 'respectable' retail chains, restaurants and attractions. By the new millennium, Times Square had gone from X-rated to G-rated, drawing almost 50 million visitors annually.

script_body: At the turn of the 20th century, Times Square was an unremarkable intersection known as Longacre Sq. That changed through a deal between subway pioneer August Belmont and New York Times publisher Adolph Ochs. Heading construction of the city's first subway line — from Lower Manhattan to Harlem — Belmont astutely realized that a Midtown business hub would encourage use of the line and maximize profit. He approached Ochs, arguing that moving to Broadway and 42nd St would be a win-win for the broadsheet: an in-house subway station would mean faster distribution of the newspaper, but also more sales to the influx of commuters. Belmont convinced mayor George B McClellan Jr to rename the square in honor of the broadsheet. In the winter of 1904–05, both the subway station and the Times' new headquarters at One Times Square made their debut.

script_body: In honor of the move, the Times hosted a New Year's Eve party in 1904, setting off fireworks from its skyscraper rooftop. By 1907 the square had become so built-up that fireworks were deemed a safety hazard, forcing the newspaper to find an alternative crowd-puller. It came as a 700lb wood-and-iron ball, lowered from the roof of One Times Square to herald the arrival of 1908. Around one million people still gather here every New Year's Eve to watch a Waterford crystal ball descend at midnight.

script_body: The neighborhood's first playhouse was the long-gone Empire, opened in 1893 on Broadway between 40th and 41st Sts. Two years later, cigar manufacturer and part-time comedy scribe Oscar Hammerstein opened the Olympia, before opening the Republic — now children's theater New Victory — in 1900. That led to a string of new venues, including the still-beating New Amsterdam Theatre and the Lyceum Theatre. The Broadway of the 1920s was known for lighthearted musicals fusing vaudeville and music-hall traditions, producing classic tunes like Cole Porter's 'Let's Misbehave.' But Midtown's theater district was also evolving as a platform for new American dramatists. One of the greatest was Eugene O'Neill, born in Times Square at the long-gone Barrett Hotel at 1500 Broadway. The playwright debuted many of his works here, including Pulitzer Prize winners Beyond the Horizon and Anna Christie. His success paved the way for other 20th-century greats — Tennessee Williams, Arthur Miller and Edward Albee — recognized by the establishment of the annual Tony Awards in 1947.

source_passage: The neighborhood's first playhouse was the long-gone Empire, opened in 1893 and located on Broadway between 40th and 41st Sts. Two years later, cigar manufacturer and part-time comedy scribe Oscar Hammerstein opened the Olympia, also on Broadway, before opening the Republic – now children's theater New Victory – in 1900. This led to a string of new venues, among them the still-beating New Amsterdam Theatre and Lyceum Theatre. The Broadway of the 1920s was well-known for its lighthearted musicals, commonly fusing vaudeville and music-hall traditions, and producing classic tunes like Cole Porter's 'Let's Misbehave.' But at the same time, Midtown's theater district was evolving as a platform for new American dramatists. One of the greatest was Eugene O'Neill (1888–1953). Born in Times Square at the long-gone Barrett Hotel (1500 Broadway), the playwright debuted many of his works here, including Pulitzer Prize winners Beyond the Horizon and Anna Christie. O'Neill's success on Broadway paved the way for other 20th-century American greats like Tennessee Williams, Arthur Miller and Edward Albee, who would come to be recognized for their serious talent by the establishment of the annual Tony Awards in 1947.

script_body: A locked, unmarked door on the 102nd-floor observation deck leads to one of New York's most outrageous pie-in-the-sky projects: a narrow terrace intended to dock zeppelins. Spearheading the dream was former New York governor Alfred E Smith, who went from failed presidential candidate in 1928 to head honcho of the Empire State Building project. When architect William Van Alen revealed the secret spire of his competing Chrysler Building, Smith went one better, declaring the Empire State Building would sport an even taller mooring mast for transatlantic airships. The plan had two major oversights: dirigibles require anchoring at both ends, not just at the nose, and passengers cannot exit the craft through the giant helium-filled balloon. That didn't stop them trying. In September 1931 the New York Evening Journal moored a zeppelin and delivered a pile of newspapers fresh out of Lower Manhattan. The docking plan never got off the ground, but years later an aircraft met the building with tragic consequences: a B-25 bomber crashed into the 79th floor on a foggy day in 1945, killing 14 people.

Gov Alfred E Smith led the project after his 1928 presidential loss
Smith planned a taller mooring mast to outdo Van Alen's Chrysler spire
Dirigible plan failed: anchoring and passenger-exit oversights
In September 1931 the NY Evening Journal moored a zeppelin
A B-25 bomber crashed into the 79th floor in 1945, killing 14
source_passage: A locked, unmarked door on the 102nd-floor observation deck leads to one of New York's most outrageous pie-in-the-sky projects to date: a narrow terrace intended to dock zeppelins. Spearheading the dream was former New York governor Alfred E Smith, who went from failed presidential candidate in 1928 to head honcho of the Empire State Building project. When architect William Van Alen revealed the secret spire of his competing Chrysler Building, Smith went one better, declaring that the top of the Empire State Building would sport an even taller mooring mast for transatlantic airships. While the plan looked good on paper, there were two (major) oversights: dirigibles require anchoring at both ends (not just at the nose, as planned) and passengers (who travel in the zeppelin's gondola) cannot exit the craft through the giant helium-filled balloon. Regardless, it didn't stop them from trying. In September 1931, the New York Evening Journal threw sanity to the wind, managing to moor a zeppelin and deliver a pile of newspapers fresh out of Lower Manhattan. Though the ambitious plan for docking airships never got off the ground, years later an aircraft met up with the building with tragic consequences: a B-25 bomber crashed into the 79th floor on a foggy day in 1945, killing 14 people.

fact_check.omission_check: Historical narrative; no change since 2022. The Sept 1931 Evening Journal delivery is a compressed account (a dirigible briefly lashed to the mast, and the Goodyear blimp Columbia delivered Evening Journals weeks later) but the book's framing of the airship-mooring-mast publicity and the newspaper delivery is substantively accurate.

script_body: MoMA boasts more A-listers than an Oscars after-party: Van Gogh, Matisse, Picasso, Warhol, Cassatt, Gauguin, Mondrian, Pollock and Bourgeois. Since its 1929 founding, the museum has amassed around 200,000 artworks, documenting creativity from the late-19th century to today. Highlights include Van Gogh's The Starry Night, usually mobbed by camera-wielding fans, Picasso's Les Demoiselles d'Avignon, Henri Rousseau's The Sleeping Gypsy, Warhol's Campbell's Soup Cans and Gold Marilyn Monroe, Matisse's Dance (I) and Hopper's poignant New York Movie.

script_body: One of MoMA's greatest strengths is abstract expressionism, a radical movement that emerged in New York in the 1940s and boomed a decade later. Defined by irreverent individualism and monumentally scaled works, this so-called New York School helped turn the metropolis into the epicenter of Western contemporary art. Among the stars on view are Mark Rothko's No. 10 (1950), Jackson Pollock's One: Number 31, 1950 and Lee Krasner's Untitled (1949).

script_body: With architect Yoshio Taniguchi's reconstruction of the museum in 2004 came the restoration of the Sculpture Garden to the original, larger vision of Philip Johnson's 1953 design. Johnson described the space as a 'sort of outdoor room.' One resident that can't seem to get enough of it is Aristide Maillol's The River, a larger-than-life female sculpture from Johnson's original garden, in fine company with works by Matisse, Giacometti, Calder and Picasso. Sitting sneakily above the garden's eastern end is Water Tower, a translucent resin installation by British artist Rachel Whiteread.

script_body: Clad in Connecticut Stony Creek granite at its base and Indiana limestone on top, Grand Central's facade is crowned by America's greatest monumental sculpture, The Glory of Commerce. Designed by French sculptor Jules-Félix Coutan and rising 48ft, it was executed in Long Island City by carvers Donnelly and Ricci, then hoisted up piece by piece in 1914. Its protagonist is a wing-capped Mercury, the Roman god of travel and commerce; to the left is Hercules in an unusually placid stance, while Minerva, the ancient guardian of cities, looks down on the mayhem of 42nd St. The clock beneath Mercury's foot contains the largest example of Tiffany glass in the world.

source_passage: Clad in Connecticut Stony Creek granite at its base and Indiana limestone on top, Grand Central's showpiece facade is crowned by America's greatest monumental sculpture, The Glory of Commerce (also known as Transportation). Designed by the French sculptor Jules-Félix Coutan and rising 48ft, the piece was executed in Long Island City by local carvers Donnelly and Ricci. Once completed, it was hoisted up, piece by piece, in 1914. Its protagonist is a wing-capped Mercury, the Roman god of travel and commerce. To the left is Hercules in an unusually placid stance, while looking down on the mayhem of 42nd St is Minerva, the ancient guardian of cities. The clock beneath Mercury's foot contains the largest example of Tiffany glass in the world.

script_body: Grand Central's centerpiece is more akin to a glorious ballroom than a thoroughfare. The marble floors are Tennessee pink, the vintage ticket counters Italian Bottocino marble. The vaulted ceiling is heavenly — its turquoise and gold-leaf mural depicting eight constellations… backwards. A mistake? Apparently not. Its French designer, painter Paul César Helleu, wished to depict the stars from God's point of view, from the outside looking in. Moisture damage saw it faithfully repainted by Charles Gulbrandsen in 1944, and renovation architects Beyer Blinder Belle later restored it, leaving a small rectangular patch of soot in the northwest corner, beneath the crab, as testament to their work.

key_claims: Floors are Tennessee pink marble, ticket counters Italian Bottocino marble

source_passage: Grand Central's centerpiece is more akin to a glorious ballroom than a thoroughfare. The marble floors are Tennessee pink, while the vintage ticket counters are Italian Bottocino marble. The vaulted ceiling is (quite literally) heavenly, its turquoise and gold-leaf mural depicting eight constellations… backwards. A mistake? Apparently not. Its French designer, painter Paul César Helleu, wished to depict the stars from God's point of view – from the out, looking in. The original, frescoed execution of Helleu's design was by New York–based artists J Monroe Hewlett and Charles Basing. Moisture damage saw it faithfully repainted (alas, not in fresco form) by Charles Gulbrandsen in 1944. By the 1990s, however, the mural was in ruins again. Enter renovation architects Beyer Blinder Belle, who restored the work, but left a small rectangular patch of soot (in the northwest corner, beneath the crab) as testament to just what a fine job they did.

fact_check.omission_check: Ceiling, backwards constellations, and the small soot patch (NW corner beneath the crab/Cancer) all confirmed present. Helleu designer, Gulbrandsen 1944 repaint, Beyer Blinder Belle restoration all documented.

script_body: The vaulted landing below the bridge linking the Main Concourse and Vanderbilt Hall is home to one of Grand Central's quirkier features, the Whispering Gallery. If you're in company, stand facing the arched corners diagonally opposite each other and whisper something. If your partner proposes — it happens a lot — chilled champagne is just through the door at the Grand Central Oyster Bar & Restaurant, hugely atmospheric with a vaulted tiled ceiling by Catalan-born engineer Rafael Guastavino. An elevator beside the restaurant leads to another historic gem, the snooty bar The Campbell.

script_body: The Chrysler Building has no restaurant or observation deck, but its lobby is a lavish consolation prize. Bathed in an amber glow, its Jazz Age vintage shows in dark, exotic African wood and marble contrasted against the brash steel of industrial America. The elaborately veneered elevators are especially beautiful, their Egyptian lotus motifs made of inlaid Japanese ash, Oriental walnut and Cuban plum-pudding wood. Above you is painter Edward Trumbull's ceiling mural Transport and Human Endeavor — purportedly the world's largest mural — depicting buildings, airplanes and workers on Chrysler assembly lines.

source_passage: Although the Chrysler Building has no restaurant or observation deck, its lobby is a lavish consolation prize. Bathed in an amber glow, its Jazz Age vintage is echoed in its architecture – dark, exotic African wood and marble, contrasted against the brash steel of industrial America. The elaborately veneered elevators are especially beautiful, their Egyptian lotus motifs made of inlaid Japanese ash, Oriental walnut and Cuban plum-pudding wood. When the doors open, you almost expect Bette Davis to strut on out. Above you is painter Edward Trumbull's ceiling mural Transport and Human Endeavor. Purportedly the world's largest mural at 97ft by 100ft, its depiction of buildings, airplanes and industrious workers on Chrysler assembly lines shows the golden promise of industry and modernity.

script_body: Composed of seven radiating steel arches reminiscent of the rising sun, the Chrysler Building's 185ft spire was as much a feat of vengeance as of engineering. Secretly constructed in the stairwell, the 200ft creation — dubbed 'the vertex' — was raised through a false roof and anchored in place in an impressive 1½ hours. The novel reveal shocked and outraged architect H Craig Severance, who had hoped his Manhattan Company skyscraper on Wall St would become the world's tallest building. The fait accompli was especially humiliating given that Severance had personally fallen out with Van Alen, a former colleague.

script_body: Balanced at the top of the Chrysler Building between 1930 and 1979 was the famed Cloud Club. Its regulars included publishing magnate Condé Montrose Nast and boxing legend Gene Tunney. The art deco–meets–hunting lodge hangout from floors 66 to 68 featured a lounge and dining rooms — including a private room for Walter Chrysler — plus kitchens, a barber shop and a locker room with sneak cabinets for hiding booze during Prohibition. Chrysler merrily boasted about having the highest toilet in town.

script_body: Across the street from the Chrysler Building, on the southwest corner of Lexington Ave and 42nd St, stands another art deco gem: the Chanin Building. Completed in 1929, the 56-story brick-and-terra-cotta tower is the work of unlicensed architect Irwin S Chanin, who teamed up with firm Sloan & Robertson. The star attraction is the work of René Chambellan and Jacques Delamarre, creators of the exquisite bands of relief at the base — birds and fish create whimsy in the lower band, while the upper band of terra-cotta steals the show with its rich botanical carvings.

source_passage: Across the street from the Chrysler Building, on the southwest corner of Lexington Ave and 42nd St, stands another art deco gem: the Chanin Building (122 E 42nd St, at Lexington Ave, Midtown East). Completed in 1929, the 56-story brick-and-terra-cotta tower is the work of unlicensed architect Irwin S Chanin, who teamed up with the legally recognized firm Sloan & Robertson to achieve his dream. Yet the star attraction here is the work of René Chambellan and Jacques Delamarre, creators of the exquisite bands of relief at the building's base. script_body: The Canarsee Native Americans called this tiny spit of land 'Minnahanonck' — Nice Island — which they sold as part of a larger parcel to the Dutch in 1633; from then it was used for livestock farming and called 'Varckens Eylandt,' Hog Island. When the British took control, the island was granted to the sheriff of New York, John Manning, and after his death passed to his stepdaughter Mrs Blackwell, becoming Blackwell's Island from the 1680s. In 1828 the city government purchased it to house various 'undesirables,' building a prison and medical facilities, including a mental-health hospital — the Octagon tower at its north end still stands — and the Renwick Smallpox Hospital, whose ruined facade haunts the island's southern half. By the mid-20th century most institutions on 'Welfare Island' had closed. In the 1970s the city renamed it for President Franklin D Roosevelt and built brutalist apartment buildings along its main road.

Renamed for FDR in the 1970s with brutalist apartments
source_passage: The Canarsee Native Americans called this tiny spit of land 'Minnahanonck' (Nice Island), which they sold as part of a larger parcel to the Dutch in 1633; from then it was used for livestock farming, and called 'Varckens Eylandt' (Hog Island). When the British took control of the area, the island was granted to the sheriff of New York, John Manning. After his death ownership transferred to his stepdaughter, Mrs Blackwell, and the island was called Blackwell's Island from the 1680s onward. In 1828 it was purchased by the city government, which used it to house various 'undesirables' by building a prison and medical facilities, including a mental-health hospital – the Octagon tower at its north end still stands as part of a residential complex – and the Renwick Smallpox Hospital, whose ruined, eerie-looking facade haunts the island's southern half. By the mid-20th century most of the institutions on 'Welfare Island' had been closed down or abandoned. In the 1970s, the city began redeveloping the island by renaming it in honor of President Franklin D Roosevelt and building a series of cookie-cutter brutalist apartment buildings along the island's main road.

fact_check.omission_check: Octagon (former asylum) and Renwick Smallpox Hospital ruin still stand; island still named for FDR. No change since 2022.

script_body: At the southern tip of Roosevelt Island, the Franklin D Roosevelt Four Freedoms Park honors America's 32nd president and his 1941 State of the Union speech. A luminous granite vision designed by architect Louis Kahn in 1973 but only completed in 2012 — 38 years after Kahn's death — it features grand stark steps leading up to a sloping triangular lawn fringed by linden trees, spilling down to a bronze bust of Roosevelt by sculptor Jo Davidson. A granite wall, hand-engraved with the speech, names the four freedoms: of speech, of worship, from want and from fear.

source_passage: At the southern tip of Roosevelt Island on the East River, this remarkable monument honors America's 32nd president and his 1941 State of the Union speech. It's breathtakingly cinematic in its scale and effect: a luminous granite vision designed by renowned architect Louis Kahn in 1973, but only completed in 2012 – 38 years after Kahn's death. A sweep of grand, stark steps lead up to a sloping triangular lawn. Fringed by linden trees, the lawn gently spills down to a bronze bust of Roosevelt by American sculptor Jo Davidson. Framing the sculpture is a granite wall, hand engraved with Roosevelt's rousing speech, in which he spoke of the four essential human freedoms he desired for the world: freedom of speech, freedom of worship, freedom from want and freedom from fear.

script_body: It's a case of 'thin is in' with 432 Park Avenue, a 1396ft-tall, $1.3-billion residential tower by Uruguayan architect Rafael Viñoly. Its clean, white, cubic facade — inspired by a 1905 trash can by Austrian designer Josef Hoffman — rises above the Midtown skyline like an impossibly slim square tube. It's one of the city's tallest buildings, surpassed by One World Trade Center, Central Park Tower, 111 West 57th Street and One Vanderbilt.

script_body: The Guggenheim came out of the collection of Solomon R. Guggenheim, a New York mining magnate who began acquiring abstract art in his 60s at the behest of his art adviser, an eccentric German baroness named Hilla Rebay. In 1939, with Rebay serving as director, Guggenheim opened a temporary museum on 54th St titled the Museum of Non-Objective Painting. Incredibly, it had grey velour walls, piped-in classical music and burning incense. Four years later, the pair commissioned Wright to construct a permanent home for the collection. Like most developments in New York City, the project took forever to come to fruition. Construction was delayed for almost 13 years due to budget constraints, the outbreak of WWII and outraged neighbors who weren't all that excited to see a giant concrete spaceship land in their midst. Construction was finally completed in 1959 — after both Wright and Guggenheim had passed away.

script_body: A sculpture in its own right, this building by architect Frank Lloyd Wright almost overshadows the collection of 20th-century art inside. Even before it opened, the inverted ziggurat structure was derided by some critics but hailed by others, who welcomed it as a beloved architectural icon. When the Guggenheim opened its doors in October 1959, the ticket price was 50¢ and the works on view included pieces by Wassily Kandinsky, Alexander Calder and abstract expressionists Franz Kline and Willem de Kooning. The structure was savaged by the New York Times, but others quickly celebrated it as one of the country's most beautiful buildings. Whether Wright intended to or not, he had given the city one of its most recognizable landmarks.

script_body: A renovation in the early 1990s added an eight-story tower to the east, which seamlessly provided an extra 20,000 sq ft of exhibition space. These galleries feature rotating exhibitions from the permanent collection, while the ramps of the Rotunda are occupied by temporary exhibits. The museum's holdings include works by Kandinsky, Picasso and Jackson Pollock. Over time, other key additions have included paintings by Monet, Van Gogh and Degas, sculpture by Constantin Brancusi, photographs by Robert Mapplethorpe, and key surrealist works donated by Guggenheim's niece Peggy. Though Wright intended visitors to go to the top and wind their way down, the cramped single elevator makes this difficult — exhibitions are installed from bottom to top.

script_body: The museum has an unrivaled collection of ancient Egyptian art, some of which dates back to the Paleolithic era. Located to the north of the Great Hall, the 39 Egyptian galleries open dramatically with one of the Met's prized pieces: the Tomb of Perneb, dating to around 2300 BCE, an Old Kingdom burial chamber crafted from limestone. From here, a web of rooms is cluttered with funerary stelae, carved reliefs and fragments of pyramids. Don't miss the intriguing models from the Tomb of Meketre, clay figurines meant to help in the afterlife, in Gallery 105. These eventually lead to the Temple of Dendur in Gallery 131, a sandstone temple to the goddess Isis given to the US by Egypt in 1965. It resides in a sunny atrium gallery with a reflecting pool — a must-see for the first-time visitor.

script_body: In the northwestern corner, the two-floor American Wing showcases a wide variety of decorative and fine art from throughout US history — from colonial portraiture to Hudson River School art, including Emanuel Leutze's massive canvas of Washington Crossing the Delaware in Gallery 760. In 2018–19, a landmark exhibition showcased 116 works of sculpture, painting, textiles and regalia from more than 50 indigenous North American cultures. The works were gifts, donations and loans from the Diker Collection, considered to be the most significant private collection of Native American art in the US.

These include everything from colonial portraiture to Hudson River School art – not to mention Emanuel Leutze's massive canvas of Washington Crossing the Delaware (Gallery 760). What the permanent collection lacks, though, is a serious body of Native American art. script_body: The 27 galleries devoted to classical antiquity are another Met highlight. From the Great Hall, a passageway takes you through a barrel-vaulted room flanked by the chiseled torsos of Greek figures. This spills right into one of the Met's loveliest spaces: the airy Greek and Roman sculpture court in Gallery 162, full of marble carvings of gods and historical figures. The statue of a bearded Hercules from 68–98 CE, with a lion's skin draped about him, is particularly awe-inspiring.
