Population reached 11,000 by the mid-1700s
source_passage: By 1664, the English showed up in battleships, ready for a fight. Stuyvesant was tired, though, and avoided bloodshed by surrendering without a shot. King Charles II promptly renamed the colony after his brother, the Duke of York. New York became a prosperous British port with a population of 11,000 by the mid-1700s. The city grew in prominence as the change point for the exchange of slaves and goods between worlds.

fact_check.omission_check: 1664 bloodless surrender of New Amsterdam by Stuyvesant; Charles II's grant to / renaming after his brother the Duke of York; growth to ~11,000 by the mid-1700s all confirmed and stable.

script_body: In 1741 a spate of fires broke out across the city, including one at Fort George — then the home of Lieutenant Governor George Clarke and the colonial fort that stood here at the foot of the island. The blazes were blamed on African-American slaves, and rumors spread of a plot by rebellious Black New Yorkers and poorer white settlers to burn down the city. Despite contradictory accounts and a lack of solid evidence, the so-called Great Negro Plot led to the arrest and execution of numerous enslaved people and their alleged co-conspirators.
key_claims: A 1741 fire struck Fort George, home of Lt Gov George Clarke
Fires blamed on slaves sparked rumors of a plot to burn the city
The Great Negro Plot led to arrests and executions despite weak evidence
source_passage: In 1741, a spate of fires occurred across the city, including one at Fort George, then home of Lieutenant Governor George Clarke. The blazes were widely blamed on African-American slaves, and rumors quickly spread of a plan by rebellious blacks and poorer white settlers to burn down New York City. Despite contradictory accounts and a lack of solid evidence, the socalled Great Negro Plot led to the arrest and execution of numerous slaves and their alleged co-conspirators.

fact_check.omission_check: No misleading omission. The 1741 fires (first at Fort George, then-home of Lt Gov/Acting Gov George Clarke, on Mar 18, 1741) and the resulting 'Great Negro Plot' arrests and executions (~13 burned, ~17+ hanged) are accurately summarized; historians do dispute whether a real plot existed, which the script acknowledges ('contradictory accounts and a lack of solid evidence').

script_body: As war loomed, Patriots clashed in public spaces with Tories loyal to the king, while Lieutenant Colonel Alexander Hamilton became a fierce anti-British organizer. Revolutionary battle began in August 1776, when General George Washington's army lost about a quarter of its men in just a couple of days. He retreated, and fire engulfed much of the colony — but the British soon left and Washington's army reclaimed the city, celebrating with banquets and fireworks here at Bowling Green.
key_claims: Revolutionary battle began August 1776; Washington lost ~a quarter of his men in days and retreated
The British later left and Washington reclaimed the city
Celebrations with banquets and fireworks were held at Bowling Green
source_passage: Patriots clashed in public spaces with Tories, who were loyal to the king, while Lieutenant Colonel Alexander Hamilton, an intellectual, became a fierce anti-British organizer. Citizens fled the city, sensing the oncoming war, and revolutionary battle began in August of 1776, when General George Washington's army lost about a quarter of its men in just a couple of days. He retreated, and fire encompassed much of the colony. But soon the British left and Washington's army reclaimed their city. After a series of celebrations, banquets and fireworks at Bowling Green, General Washington bade farewell to his officers at what is now the Fraunces Tavern Museum and retired as commander in chief.

fact_check.omission_check: No misleading omission. Battle of Brooklyn/Long Island began Aug 27, 1776; American losses (~300 killed, 650 wounded, ~1,100 captured of ~10,000 engaged) make 'about a quarter of his men' a defensible Lonely Planet approximation. Washington's overnight retreat (Aug 29-30) to Manhattan, the Great Fire of Sept 1776, and the British departure on Evacuation Day 1783 with Washington reclaiming the city are all accurate.
unverified_claims: The specific detail of banquets and fireworks celebrated 'here at Bowling Green' (local color from Lonely Planet; not independently corroborated, though consistent with 1783 Evacuation Day celebrations)

script_body: After the Revolution, Alexander Hamilton became Washington's secretary of the treasury and set about rebuilding New York — his financial program laying the groundwork for the New York Stock Exchange. But people distrusted a capital sitting next to the financial power of Wall St merchants, and New Yorkers soon lost the seat of the presidency to Philadelphia.
key_claims: Hamilton became Washington's treasury secretary and worked to establish the NYSE
Distrust of a capital beside Wall St merchants cost New York the presidency to Philadelphia
source_passage: Alexander Hamilton, meanwhile, began rebuilding New York and became Washington's secretary of the treasury, working to establish the New York Stock Exchange. But people distrusted a capitol located adjacent to the financial power of Wall St merchants, and New Yorkers lost the seat of the presidency to Philadelphia shortly thereafter.

fact_check.omission_check: Dispute resolved by edit (Category B/C/D).

corrections.original_text: working to establish the New York Stock Exchange
corrections.corrected_text: his financial program laying the groundwork for the New York Stock Exchange

script_body: On December 16, 1835, a gas line broke in a dry-goods store near Hanover Square. The fire spread fast — south down Stone St and northeast toward Wall St — and raged for over a day, destroying much of what remained of the original Dutch and British colonial city.
key_claims: On Dec 16, 1835 a gas-line break near Hanover Square started a fire
It spread south down Stone St and northeast toward Wall St, raging over a day
It destroyed much of the original Dutch and British colonial city
source_passage: On December 16, 1835, a gas line broke in a dry-goods store near Hanover Square, causing a massive fire to quickly spread south down Stone St and northeast toward Wall St. Raging for over a day, it destroyed much of what remained of the original Dutch and British colonial city.

fact_check.omission_check: No misleading omission. The Great Fire of New York began the evening of Dec 16, 1835, from a ruptured gas pipe igniting in the Comstock & Andrews dry-goods store near Hanover Square (Beaver/Hanover/Wall area); it raged through the bitter-cold night into the next day, destroyed ~700 buildings across ~17 blocks, and leveled much of the old Dutch/British colonial core. The directional spread (south down Stone St, northeast toward Wall St) is consistent with the affected district.

script_body: The 19th century brought hard setbacks — the Great Fire of 1835, the bloody Draft Riots of 1863, massive cholera epidemics, and the serious poverty and crime of Five Points, the city's first slum, which stood right where Chinatown now lies.
key_claims: Five Points was the city's first slum
It stood where Chinatown now lies
source_passage: The 19th century brought with it plenty of setbacks: the Great Fire of 1835, the bloody Draft Riots of 1863, massive cholera epidemics, rising tensions among 'old' and new immigrants, and the serious poverty and crime of Five Points, the city's first slum, located where Chinatown now lies.

fact_check.omission_check: No misleading omission. Five Points is widely described as the city's (and America's) first/most notorious slum, centered on the Baxter/Worth/Mosco intersection in what is today Chinatown / Columbus Park. Surrounding context (Great Fire of 1835, Draft Riots of 1863, cholera epidemics) is accurate.

script_body: Central Park was conceived as a grand project to boost the health of people crammed into tiny tenement apartments — an 843-acre public park. Work began in 1855 in an area so far uptown that some immigrants kept pigs, sheep and goats on the land. From the start the park was both a vision of green reform and a boon to real-estate speculation.
key_claims: Central Park was an 843-acre public park begun in 1855
The area was so far uptown some immigrants kept pigs, sheep and goats there
It was both green reform and a boon to real-estate speculation
source_passage: And there was yet another grand project afoot – one to boost the health of the people crammed into tiny tenement apartments – in the form of an 843acre public park. Begun in 1855 in an area so far uptown that some immigrants kept pigs, sheep and goats there, Central Park was both a vision of green reform and a boon to real-estate speculation.

fact_check.omission_check: No misleading omission. Central Park is 843 acres. The 'Work began in 1855' date is defensible: the city began the land-acquisition/eviction process for the park around 1853-1856, though physical construction proper began in 1857 (a ~2-year nuance, not a clear error). Pre-park land was occupied by ~1,600 residents including squatters who kept hogs/goats; the dual framing of green reform plus real-estate speculation is accurate.

script_body: German-born engineer John Roebling set out to solve the winter freezes that kept shutting down the ferry between downtown Manhattan and Brooklyn, then an independent city. He designed a soaring symphony of spun wire and Gothic arches to span the East River, and his Brooklyn Bridge accelerated the fusion of the neighboring cities.

physical_cues.cue: The spun-wire cables and Gothic arches spanning the East River

key_claims: Roebling sought to solve winter freezes that shut down the Manhattan-Brooklyn ferry
He designed a bridge of spun wire and Gothic arches over the East River
The bridge accelerated the fusion of the two cities
source_passage: Another vision was realized by German-born engineer John Roebling, who sought a solution to a series of winter freezes that had shut down the ferry system connecting downtown Manhattan to Brooklyn, then an independent city. He designed a soaring symphony of spun wire and Gothic arches to span the East River, and his Brooklyn Bridge accelerated the fusion of the neighboring cities.

fact_check.omission_check: No misleading omission. John A. Roebling was a German-born (Prussian) engineer and suspension-bridge/wire-rope pioneer who designed the Brooklyn Bridge over the East River, connecting Manhattan with Brooklyn (then an independent city until 1898 consolidation). The bridge's spun-wire cables and Gothic-arched stone towers still stand and span the East River. The 'winter freezes shutting down the ferry' motivation is the book's framing and is plausible (the East River was known to freeze in hard winters).

script_body: The Brooklyn Bridge opened with fanfare on May 24, 1883. After New York mayor Franklin Edson and Brooklyn mayor Seth Low led President Chester Arthur and Governor Grover Cleveland across, more than 150,000 members of the public followed — each paying a penny for the honor.
key_claims: The bridge opened May 24, 1883
Mayors Edson and Low led President Arthur and Governor Cleveland across
More than 150,000 people crossed, each paying a penny
source_passage: New York's Brooklyn Bridge opened with suitable fanfare on May 24, 1883. After New York mayor Franklin Edson and Brooklyn mayor Seth Low led President Chester Arthur and Governor Grover Cleveland across the structure, more than 150,000 members of the public followed suit, each paying a penny for the honor.

fact_check.omission_check: No misleading omission. The Brooklyn Bridge opened May 24, 1883. NY Mayor Franklin Edson and Brooklyn Mayor Seth Low led the ceremonial crossing with President Chester A. Arthur and NY Governor Grover Cleveland. More than 150,000 people streamed across in the first 24 hours; pedestrian toll was one penny (5c horse-and-rider, 10c horse-and-wagon).

script_body: By the turn of the 20th century, elevated trains carried a million people a day in and out of the city, and the metropolis overflowed with immigrants arriving from southern Italy and Eastern Europe — boosting the population to around three million. The journey from the immigrant landing stations at Castle Garden and Ellis Island led straight to the Lower East Side, where streets reflected these myriad origins with shop signs in Yiddish, Italian, German and Chinese.
key_claims: By 1900 elevated trains carried a million people a day; population reached ~3 million
Immigrants arrived from southern Italy and Eastern Europe via Castle Garden and Ellis Island
They settled the Lower East Side with shop signs in Yiddish, Italian, German and Chinese
source_passage: By the turn of the 20th century, elevated trains carried one million people a day in and out of the city. At this point, the city was simply overflowing with the masses of immigrants arriving from southern Italy and Eastern Europe, who had boosted the metropolis's population to around three million. The journey from immigrant landing stations at Castle Garden and Ellis Island led straight to the Lower East Side. There, streets reflected these myriad origins with shop signs in Yiddish, Italian, German and Chinese.

fact_check.omission_check: Historical narrative; no post-2022 change affects it.

script_body: By the late 19th century all sorts of folks were living in squalor — crammed into packed tenements, shivering in soup lines and shoveling snow for nickels — while newly wealthy financiers built European-style chateaux on Fifth Ave. Reporter and photographer Jacob Riis exposed the widening gap between the classes in the New York Tribune and in his now-classic 1890 book, How the Other Half Lives, eventually forcing the city to pass much-needed housing reforms.
key_claims: Late-19th-century poor crammed into tenements while the wealthy built Fifth Ave chateaux
Jacob Riis exposed the class gap in the New York Tribune and his 1890 book How the Other Half Lives
His work forced the city to pass housing reforms
source_passage: All sorts of folks were living in squalor by the late 19th century, when the immigration processing center at Ellis Island opened, welcoming one million newcomers in just its first year. They crammed into packed tenements, shivered in soup lines and shoveled snow for nickels. Reporter and photographer Jacob Riis illuminated the widening gap between the classes by writing about it in the New York Tribune and in his now-classic 1890 book, How the Other Half Lives, eventually forcing the city to pass much-needed housing reforms.

fact_check.omission_check: Historical narrative; Riis dates and Tribune affiliation confirmed.

script_body: Alongside the suffragists holding street-corner rallies for the vote, nurse and midwife Margaret Sanger opened the first birth-control clinic in Brooklyn — where 'purity police' promptly arrested her. After her release from jail in 1921, she formed the American Birth Control League, now Planned Parenthood, which provided services for young women and researched safe methods of birth control.
key_claims: Margaret Sanger opened the first birth-control clinic in Brooklyn and was arrested by 'purity police'
After release in 1921 she formed the American Birth Control League, now Planned Parenthood
source_passage: Nurse and midwife Margaret Sanger opened the first birth-control clinic in Brooklyn, where 'purity police' promptly arrested her. After her release from jail in 1921 she formed the American Birth Control League (now Planned Parenthood), which provided services for young women and researched methods of safe birth control.

fact_check.omission_check: Sanger opened the first US birth control clinic in Brownsville, Brooklyn (Oct 1916), was arrested; founded American Birth Control League 1921 (precursor to Planned Parenthood). Confirmed.

script_body: The 1920s brought the Jazz Age, when Prohibition outlawed alcohol and fueled bootlegging, speakeasies and organized crime. As the Great Migration carried Black Americans north from the South, Harlem became the center of the Harlem Renaissance — a flowering of poetry, music and painting whose innovative spirit still inspires. Harlem's daring nightlife in the '20s and '30s drew the flappers and gin-soaked revelers who marked the complete failure of Prohibition and foreshadowed the liberated nightlife New Yorkers enjoy today.
key_claims: The 1920s Jazz Age and Prohibition fueled bootlegging and speakeasies
The Great Migration made Harlem the center of the Harlem Renaissance
Harlem's '20s-'30s nightlife marked Prohibition's failure
source_passage: The 1920s saw the dawning of the Jazz Age, when Prohibition outlawed the sale of alcohol, encouraging bootlegging and speakeasies, as well as organized crime. Babe Ruth reigned at Yankee Stadium and the Great Migration from the South led to the Harlem Renaissance, when the neighborhood became a center of African American culture and society. It produced poetry, music, painting and an innovative attitude that continues to influence and inspire. Harlem's daring nightlife in the 1920s and '30s attracted the flappers and gin-soaked revelers who marked the complete failure of Prohibition, and provided a foretaste of the liberated nightlife New Yorkers enjoy today.

fact_check.omission_check: Canonical history: Prohibition (1920-33), Great Migration, Harlem Renaissance. No issue.

script_body: When the stock market crashed in 1929, the Great Depression descended, and the once-grand Central Park blossomed with shacks derisively called Hoovervilles, after the president who refused to help the needy. The city scraped through on grit, rent parties and public-works projects, until Mayor Fiorello La Guardia found a friend in President Franklin Roosevelt and worked his Washington connections to bring relief money home.
key_claims: The 1929 crash brought the Great Depression
Central Park filled with shacks called Hoovervilles after President Hoover
Mayor La Guardia worked with FDR to bring relief money to the city
source_passage: The stock market crashed in 1929, beginning the Great Depression of the 1930s, which the city dealt with through a combination of grit, endurance, rent parties, militancy and a slew of public-works projects. The once-grand Central Park blossomed with shacks, derisively called Hoovervilles, after the president who refused to help the needy. But Mayor Fiorello La Guardia found a friend in President Franklin Roosevelt, and worked his Washington connections to great effect to bring relief money – and subsequent prosperity – home.

fact_check.omission_check: 1929 crash, Central Park Hooverville on the drained Lower Reservoir (Great Lawn), La Guardia-FDR relief ties all confirmed.

script_body: World War II brought troops galore to the city, ready to party down to their last dollar in Times Square before being shipped off to Europe. As the local factories converted to war industries and hummed — newly staffed by women and African American workers — the wartime boom created a housing crunch that gave New York its much-imitated, tenant-protecting Rent Control Law.
key_claims: WWII troops partied in Times Square before shipping to Europe
War factories were staffed by women and African American workers
The wartime housing crunch produced NYC's Rent Control Law
source_passage: WWII brought troops galore to the city, ready to party down to their last dollar in Times Square, before being shipped off to Europe. Converted to war industries, the local factories hummed, staffed by women and African American workers who had rarely had access to good, unionized jobs. The explosion of wartime activity led to a huge housing crunch that brought New York its much-imitated, tenant-protecting Rent Control Law.

fact_check.omission_check: NYC rent control originated 1943 from WWII housing shortage (Emergency Price Control Act); NY was the famed exception that retained it ('much-imitated'). Confirmed.

script_body: As Midtown bulked up with postwar skyscrapers and the financial center marched north, banker David Rockefeller and his brother, Governor Nelson Rockefeller, dreamed up the Twin Towers as a way to revitalize downtown.
key_claims: David Rockefeller and Governor Nelson Rockefeller dreamed up the Twin Towers to revitalize downtown
source_passage: There were few evident controls on business, as Midtown bulked up with skyscrapers after the war. The financial center marched north, while banker David Rockefeller and his brother, Governor Nelson Rockefeller, dreamed up the Twin Towers to revitalize downtown.

fact_check.omission_check: David Rockefeller (Chase chairman, DLMA) and brother Gov. Nelson Rockefeller championed the WTC to revitalize downtown; towers nicknamed 'David and Nelson'. Confirmed.

script_body: No one shaped the physical city of the 20th century more than urban planner Robert Moses — wonderfully or tragically, depending on whom you ask. He was the mastermind behind the Triborough Bridge, the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge, the West Side Hwy and the Long Island parkway system, plus endless highways, tunnels and bridges. His vision did away with intimate neighborhoods of brownstones and town houses in favor of sweeping parks and soaring towers — and his efforts to bulldoze neighborhoods so enraged preservationists that their pushback led to the Landmarks Preservation Commission being formed in 1965.
key_claims: Robert Moses shaped the 20th-century city more than anyone
He built the Triborough Bridge, Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge, West Side Hwy and Long Island parkways
Preservationist pushback against his demolitions led to the 1965 Landmarks Preservation Commission
source_passage: Robert Moses, an urban planner who would influence the physical shape of the city more than anyone else in the 20th century – either wonderfully or tragically, depending on whom you ask. He was the mastermind behind the Triborough Bridge (now the Robert F Kennedy Bridge), Jones Beach State Park, the Verrazzano–Narrows Bridge, the West Side Hwy and the Long Island parkway system – not to mention endless highways, tunnels and bridges. His vision was one of doing away with intimate neighborhoods of brownstones and town houses, and of creating sweeping parks and soaring towers. The approach got preservationists fired up and their efforts to stop him from bulldozing neighborhoods led to the Landmarks Preservation Commission being formed in 1965.

fact_check.omission_check: Moses built Triborough & Verrazzano-Narrows bridges, West Side Hwy, LI parkways; NYC Landmarks Preservation Commission created April 15, 1965 amid the preservation backlash (Penn Station). Confirmed.

script_body: The 1950s and '60s ushered in an era of legendary creativity and anti-establishment expression centered in Greenwich Village. One movement was abstract expressionism, a large-scale outbreak of American painters — Mark Rothko, Jackson Pollock and Helen Frankenthaler among them — who offended and intrigued with incomprehensible squiggles and exuberant energy. Then there were the writers: Beat poets Allen Ginsberg and Jack Kerouac and novelist-playwright Jane Bowles, who gathered in Village coffeehouses to exchange ideas, often finding inspiration in the folk music of burgeoning names such as Bob Dylan.
key_claims: The 1950s-60s creative era centered in Greenwich Village
Abstract expressionists included Rothko, Pollock and Frankenthaler
Beat writers Ginsberg, Kerouac and Bowles gathered in Village coffeehouses, drawn to folk music like Bob Dylan's
source_passage: The 1950s and '60s ushered in an era of legendary creativity and antiestablishment expression, with many of its creators centered in Greenwich Village. One movement was abstract expressionism, a large-scale outbreak of American painters – Mark Rothko, Jackson Pollock and Helen Frankenthaler among them – who offended and intrigued with incomprehensible squiggles, blotches and exuberant energy. Then there were the writers, such as Beat poets Allen Ginsberg and Jack Kerouac and novelist/playwright Jane Bowles. They gathered in Village coffeehouses to exchange ideas and find inspiration, which was often found in the form of folk music from burgeoning big names, such as Bob Dylan.

fact_check.omission_check: Historical 1950s-60s account; no superseding event affects accuracy.
unverified_claims: That Jane Bowles specifically gathered in Village coffeehouses with the Beats (Bowles spent the 1950s-60s mostly abroad in Tangier; she frequented Greenwich Village bohemia in the 1930s-40s). The book's grouping is loose but the figures and movements named are all correctly associated with the Village creative scene.

script_body: By the early 1970s, deficits had created a serious fiscal crisis that effectively demoted Mayor Abraham Beame to a figurehead. President Ford's refusal to lend federal aid — summed up by the Daily News headline 'Ford to City, Drop Dead' — marked the nadir of the relationship between the US and the city it loved to hate. Massive layoffs decimated the working class, and untended bridges, roads and parks reeked of hard times.
key_claims: Early-1970s deficits demoted Mayor Beame to a figurehead
Ford refused federal aid; the Daily News ran 'Ford to City, Drop Dead'
Layoffs decimated the working class and infrastructure decayed
source_passage: By the early 1970s, deficits had created a serious fiscal crisis, effectively demoting the elected mayor Abraham Beame to a figurehead, turning over the city's real financial power to Governor Carey and his appointees. President Ford's refusal to lend federal aid – summed up nicely by the Daily News headline 'Ford to City, Drop Dead' – marked the nadir of the relationship between the US and the city it loved to hate. As massive layoffs decimated the city's working class, untended bridges, roads and parks reeked of hard times.

fact_check.omission_check: Settled 1970s history; Daily News headline ran Oct 30, 1975 after Ford's Oct 29 speech. No omission.

script_body: The traumatic '70s — which hit bottom in 1977 with a citywide blackout and the terrorizing serial killer David Berkowitz — saw rents fall, which nourished an exciting alternative culture. Artists staged performances in abandoned schools, opened galleries in unused storefronts and revived the hair-dye industry with the punk-rock aesthetic. Ramones-loving punks turned former warehouses into pulsing meccas of nightlife, transforming the old industrial precincts of SoHo and Tribeca into America's center of tattooing and independent filmmaking.
key_claims: The 1977 blackout and serial killer David Berkowitz marked the decade's low point
Falling rents nourished an alternative punk culture
Punks transformed SoHo and Tribeca warehouses into nightlife and the center of tattooing and indie filmmaking
source_passage: The traumatic '70s – which reached a low point in 1977 with a citywide blackout and terrorizing serial killer David Berkowitz – saw rents fall, which helped nourish an exciting alternative culture that staged performances in abandoned schools, opened galleries in unused storefronts and breathed new life into the hair-dye industry with the advent of the punk-rock aesthetic. Ramones-loving punks turned former warehouses into pulsing meccas of nightlife, transforming the former industrial precincts of SoHo and Tribeca.

fact_check.omission_check: 1977 blackout and Son of Sam (David Berkowitz) are well-documented; cultural characterization is the book's own framing. No omission.

script_body: During the 1970s a wave of arson attacks reduced blocks of apartment houses in the South Bronx to cinders. Amid the smoke, an influential hip-hop culture was born, fueled by the percussive rhythms of Puerto Rican salsa. Rock Steady Crew, led by 'Crazy Legs' Richie Colon, pioneered athletic, competitive break dancing; DJ Kool Herc spun vinyl for all-night break-beat parties; and Afrika Bambaataa, another founding hip-hop DJ, formed Zulu Nation, bringing DJs, break dancers and graffiti writers together to end violence.
key_claims: 1970s arson reduced South Bronx apartment blocks to cinders
Hip-hop was born there, fueled by Puerto Rican salsa
Rock Steady Crew, DJ Kool Herc and Afrika Bambaataa's Zulu Nation were founding forces
source_passage: During the 1970s a wave of arson attacks reduced blocks of apartment houses in the South Bronx to cinders. Amid the smoke, an influential hiphop culture was born, fueled by the percussive rhythms of Puerto Rican salsa. Rock Steady Crew, led by 'Crazy Legs' Richie Colón, pioneered athletic, competitive break dancing. DJ Kool Herc spun vinyl for break beat all-night dance parties. Afrika Bambaataa, another founding hip-hop DJ, formed Zulu Nation, bringing DJs, break dancers and graffiti writers together to end violence.

fact_check.omission_check: South Bronx hip-hop origin story is well-established; Kool Herc, Bambaataa, Zulu Nation and Rock Steady Crew all correctly named. No omission.
unverified_claims: Crazy Legs (Richie Colon) is documented as co-founder and president of Rock Steady Crew; 'led by' is a reasonable characterization for the crew's most prominent figure rather than the original founder.

script_body: Daring graffiti dazzled the public with train-long graphics. The best-known 'masterpiece' belied the writers' reputation as vandals: Lee 163, with the Fab 5 crew, painted a whole subway car with the message 'Merry Christmas, New York.' Some of these maestros of the spray can infiltrated the art world — most notably Jean-Michel Basquiat.
key_claims: Lee 163, with the Fab 5 crew, painted a whole subway car reading 'Merry Christmas, New York'
Some graffiti writers entered the art world, notably Jean-Michel Basquiat
source_passage: Daring examples of graffiti dazzled the public with train-long graphics. The best-known 'masterpiece' belied the graf writers' reputation as vandals: Lee 163, with the Fab 5 crew, painted a whole car of trains with the message 'Merry Christmas, New York.' Some of these maestros of the spray can infiltrated the art world, most notably Jean-Michel Basquiat.

fact_check.omission_check: Lee Quinones (a.k.a. Lee 163) and Fab 5 whole-car subway works, and Basquiat's crossover to the fine-art world, are well-documented. No omission.
unverified_claims: The specific 'Merry Christmas, New York' whole-car piece is cited in the book but I could not independently corroborate that exact title; Lee Quinones is well-documented painting whole subway cars with the Fab 5, and a holiday-themed whole car is consistent with his oeuvre.

script_body: After the early-1990s real-estate crash, the dot-com market roared in, turning geeks into millionaires and the New York Stock Exchange into a speculator's fun park. Buoyed by tax receipts from IPO profits, the city launched a frenzy of building and partying unparalleled since the 1920s. With pro-business Mayor Rudy Giuliani targeting high-crime areas and using statistics to focus police, crime dropped, restaurants boomed and New York became America's safest big city — though things were faltering again as the new millennium dawned.
key_claims: The dot-com market turned the NYSE into a speculator's fun park
IPO tax receipts funded a 1920s-scale building and partying frenzy
Giuliani's statistics-driven policing made New York America's safest big city
source_passage: And then the dot-com market roared in, turning geeks into millionaires and the New York Stock Exchange into a speculator's fun park. Buoyed by tax receipts from IPO (initial public offering) profits, the city launched a frenzy of building, boutique-ing and partying unparalleled since the 1920s. The energetic mayor succeeded in making New York America's safest big city, by targeting highcrime areas and using statistics to focus police presence. Crime dropped, restaurants boomed, real-estate prices sizzled, and Sex & the City beamed a vision of sophisticated singles in Manolos around the world. Still, things were faltering in New York at the dawn of the new millennium.

fact_check.omission_check: Dot-com boom and Giuliani-era CompStat crime decline are documented; FBI recognized NYC as the safest large city in the late 1990s. Note Giuliani is a living person but the historical policy/crime claims here are factual, not contested character claims. No omission.

script_body: On September 11, 2001, terrorists flew two hijacked planes into the World Trade Center's Twin Towers, turning the whole complex to dust and rubble and killing nearly 3000 people. Downtown Manhattan took months to recover from the ghastly fumes wafting from the ruins, as forlorn missing-person posters grew ragged on brick walls. While the city mourned its dead and recovery crews coughed through the debris, residents braved constant terrorist alerts and an anthrax scare — yet shock and grief drew people together, uniting the often fractious citizenry in a determined effort not to succumb to despair.
key_claims: On Sept 11, 2001 two hijacked planes hit the Twin Towers, killing nearly 3000
Downtown took months to recover from fumes; missing-person posters covered walls
Grief united the citizenry against despair
source_passage: On September 11, 2001, terrorists flew two hijacked planes into the World Trade Center's Twin Towers, turning the whole complex to dust and rubble and killing nearly 3000 people. Downtown Manhattan took months to recover from the ghastly fumes wafting from the ruins as forlorn missingperson posters grew ragged on brick walls. While the city mourned its dead and recovery crews coughed their way through the debris, residents braved constant terrorist alerts and an anthrax scare. Shock and grief drew people together, uniting the oft-fractious citizenry in a determined effort not to succumb to despair.

fact_check.omission_check: Sept 11, 2001 attacks and ~2,977 deaths at WTC/total are settled history. No omission.

script_body: In 2012, superstorm Hurricane Sandy struck New York. A prestorm surge on October 28 turned parts of Brooklyn and New Jersey into a New World Venice, but Sandy saved her ultimate blow for the next day — cyclonic winds and drenching rain caused severe flooding and property damage, including to the subway system, the Hugh L Carey Tunnel and the World Trade Center site. A major power blackout plunged much of Lower Manhattan into surreal darkness, and trading at the New York Stock Exchange was suspended for two days.
key_claims: Hurricane Sandy hit NYC in 2012; an Oct 28 prestorm surge flooded Brooklyn and New Jersey
Sandy caused severe flooding to the subway, Hugh L Carey Tunnel and WTC site

script_body: Bagels may have been invented in Europe, but they were perfected around the turn of the 19th century in New York City — and once you've had one here, you'll have a hard time enjoying one anywhere else. It's a ring of plain-yeast dough that's first boiled and then baked, and bagel-makers claim it's the New York water that adds an elusive sweetness never found anywhere else. The most traditionally New York way to order is by asking for a 'bagel and a schmear' — said bagel with a small but thick swipe of cream cheese. Or splurge and add some lox — thinly sliced smoked salmon — as was originally sold from pushcarts on the Lower East Side by Jewish immigrants back in the early 1900s.

source_passage: Bagels may have been invented in Europe, but they were perfected around the turn of the 19th century in NYC – and once you've had one here, you'll have a hard time enjoying one anywhere else. It's a straightforward masterpiece: a ring of plain-yeast dough that's first boiled and then baked, either left plain or topped with various finishing touches, from sesame seeds to chocolate chips. 'Bagels' made in other parts of the country are often just baked and not boiled, which makes them nothing more than a roll with a hole. And even if they do get boiled elsewhere, bagel-makers here claim that it's the New York water that adds an elusive sweetness never to be found anywhere else. The most traditionally New York way to order one is by asking for a 'bagel and a schmear,' which will yield you said bagel with a small but thick swipe of cream cheese. Or splurge and add some lox – thinly sliced smoked salmon – as was originally sold from pushcarts on the Lower East Side by Jewish immigrants back in the early 1900s.

script_body: The key ingredient in New York–style cheesecake — cream cheese — came from a mistake. A botched attempt at making French Neufchâtel cheese by a 19th-century New York farmer resulted in a curious product. Enter James Kraft, founder of Kraft Foods, who picked it up in 1912, reformulated it, wrapped it in foil and introduced the country to cream cheese. Classic New York cheesecake was then immortalized at Lindy's restaurant in Midtown, opened by Leo Lindemann in 1921, where the particular confection — cream cheese, heavy cream, a dash of vanilla and a cookie crust — became wildly popular in the 1940s. Today, the most famous version is Junior's, right here in Downtown Brooklyn, whose well-known fans include Barack Obama.

Classic New York cheesecake would be immortalized by Lindy's restaurant in Midtown. script_body: Another New York classic was born in 1874 — the summer-centric Tom Collins. A mix of dry gin, sugar, lemon juice and club soda, the long drink's name stems from an elaborate hoax in which hundreds of locals were informed that a certain Tom Collins had been sullying their good names. While many set out to track him down, clued-in bartenders relished the joke by making the drink and naming it for the fictitious troublemaker. When the aggrieved stormed into the bars looking for a Tom Collins, they were served the drink to cool their tempers.

script_body: Beer brewing was once a thriving industry in Brooklyn — by the 1870s, the borough boasted a belly-swelling 48 breweries. Most of these were based in Williamsburg, Bushwick and Greenpoint, neighborhoods packed with German immigrants with extensive brewing know-how. By the eve of Prohibition in 1919, the borough was one of the country's leading beer peddlers, famous for kids carrying growlers — beer jugs — as for its bridges. By the end of Prohibition in 1933, most breweries had shut shop. Fast-forward to today and Brooklyn is once more a catchword for craft beer, led by Brooklyn Brewery, brewing IPAs, lagers, non-alcoholic beers and limited-release offerings like raspberry sour ale.

By the end of Prohibition in 1933, most breweries had shut shop. And while the industry rose from the ashes in WWII, local flavor gave in to big-gun Midwestern brands. Fast-forward to today and Brooklyn is once more a catchword for a decent brewski as a handful of craft breweries put integrity back on tap. script_body: In the 1940s, an influx of cultural figures fleeing the carnage of WWII saturated New York City with fresh ideas. Peggy Guggenheim established the Art of this Century gallery on 57th St, a space that helped launch the careers of painters such as Jackson Pollock, Willem de Kooning and Robert Motherwell. script_body: Contemporary graffiti as we know it was cultivated in NYC. In the 1970s, the graffiti-covered subway train became a potent symbol of the city and work by figures such as Dondi, Blade and Lady Pink became known around the world. Fine artists such as Jean-Michel Basquiat, Kenny Scharf and Keith Haring began incorporating elements of graffiti into their work. The movement received new life in the late 1990s when a new generation of artists — many with art-school pedigrees — began using cut paper and sculptural elements. Less celebratory was the 2013 closure of the iconic 5Pointz, a cluster of Long Island City warehouses dripping with Technicolor graffiti — not even a plea from legendary British artist Banksy could save the veritable gallery, condemned to demolition. Today, spray-can and stencil hot spots include the Brooklyn side of the Williamsburg Bridge and the corner of Troutman St and St Nicholas Ave in Bushwick.

The movement received new life in the late 1990s when a new generation of artists – many with art-school pedigrees – began using materials such as cut paper and sculptural elements. Well-known New York City artists working in this vein include John Fekner, Stephen 'ESPO' Powers, Swoon, and the twin-brother duo Skewville and Shepard Fairey, who later went on to create the Obama 'Hope' poster. Less celebratory was the 2013 closure of the iconic 5Pointz, a cluster of Long Island City warehouses dripping with Technicolor graffiti. Not even a plea from legendary British artist Banksy could save the veritable gallery, condemned to demolition. script_body: New York City has been a magnet for musicians across every genre. The city was where jazz players such as Ornette Coleman, Miles Davis and John Coltrane pushed the limits of improvisation in the 1950s; where folk singers Bob Dylan and Joan Baez crooned protest songs in coffeehouses; where bands such as the New York Dolls and the Ramones tore up the stage in Manhattan's gritty downtown; the nerve center of disco; and the cultural crucible where hip-hop was nurtured and grew. The local indie-rock scene is especially vibrant — groups including the Yeah Yeah Yeahs, LCD Soundsystem and Animal Collective all emerged in NYC, with Williamsburg at the heart of the action, packed with clubs, bars, indie record labels and internet radio stations.

script_body: In the early 20th century, clusters of theaters settled into the area around Times Square and began producing popular plays and suggestive comedies, with roots in early vaudeville. By the 1920s, these works had evolved into on-stage spectacles like Show Boat, an all-out Oscar Hammerstein production about the lives of performers on a Mississippi steamboat. In 1943, Broadway had its first runaway hit — Oklahoma! — that remained on stage for a record 2212 performances. Today, Broadway musicals are shown in one of 41 official Broadway theaters, lavish early-20th-century jewels surrounding Times Square.

script_body: For nearly 100 years, New York City has been at the center of American dance. The American Ballet Theatre — founded by Lucia Chase and Richard Pleasant — was founded in 1939 and promoted the idea of cultivating American talent, hiring native-born dancers and putting on works by choreographers such as Jerome Robbins, Twyla Tharp and Alvin Ailey. NYC is also known for nurturing a generation of modern-dance choreographers such as Martha Graham, who challenged traditional notions of dance with boxy, industrial movements on bare, almost abstract sets. The boundaries were pushed further by Merce Cunningham, who disassociated dance from music.

The company continues to perform in New York and around the world. But NYC is perhaps best known for nurturing a generation of modern-dance choreographers – figures such as Martha Graham, who challenged traditional notions of dance with boxy, industrial movements on bare, almost abstract sets. script_body: The city that is home to the country's biggest publishing houses has also been home to some of its best-known writers. In the 19th century, Herman Melville (Moby Dick), Edith Wharton (The House of Mirth) and Walt Whitman (Leaves of Grass) all congregated here. Literary life became even more exciting in the early 20th century — there were the liquor-fueled literary salons of poet-communist John Reed in the 1910s, the acerbic wisecracks of the Algonquin Round Table in the 1920s, and the thinly veiled novels of Dawn Powell in the '40s, whose work often critiqued New York's media establishment.

Poet Langston Hughes examined the condition of African Americans in Harlem, while Beat poets such as Allen Ginsberg rejected traditional rhyme in favor of free-flowing musings. script_body: Today the arts scene in New York is mixed and wide-ranging. The major institutions — the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Museum of Modern Art, the Whitney Museum of American Art, the Guggenheim Museum, and the Brooklyn Museum — deliver major retrospectives covering everything from Renaissance portraiture to contemporary installation. The New Museum of Contemporary Art, on the Lower East Side, is more daring. New York remains the world's gallery capital, with well over 1000 spaces showcasing all kinds of art across the city.

script_body: A number of gay-owned businesses once lined MacDougal St, among them the legendary Eve's Hangout at number 129, a tearoom run by Polish Jewish immigrant Eva Kotchever, known as Eve Addams. Police raided the place in June 1926, charging Eve with 'obscenity' for penning her Lesbian Love anthology and deporting her to Europe. There she ran a bookstore and club in Paris, fought in the Spanish Civil War, and was eventually imprisoned and murdered in Auschwitz. Playwright Barbara Kahn wrote Unreachable Eden about Kotchever's life.

script_body: Harlem's drag balls became a hit with gay and straight New Yorkers in the roaring '20s. The biggest was the Hamilton Lodge Ball, run by Lodge #710 of the Grand United Order of Odd Fellows and held annually at the swank Rockland Palace on 155th St. Commonly dubbed the Faggots Ball, it let men and women legally cross-dress and steal a same-sex dance, with a beauty pageant crowning the 'Queen of the Ball.' Langston Hughes called it the 'spectacles of color,' and the gay writer was one of many literati to attend; the papers covered the outrageous frocks as the talk of the town.

script_body: By the 1940s and '50s, the relative transgression of the early 20th century had given way to a new conservatism — the Great Depression, WWII and the Cold War took their toll, and Senator Joseph McCarthy declared that homosexuals in the State Department threatened America's security and children. Tougher policing forced the queer scene underground, and crackdowns on gay venues grew increasingly common. Yet on June 28, 1969, when police raided the Stonewall Inn — a gay-friendly watering hole in Greenwich Village — patrons did the unthinkable: they revolted. Fed up with harassment and with corrupt officers taking payoffs from the bars' mostly organized-crime owners, they bombarded the police with coins, bottles, bricks and chants of 'gay power' and 'we shall overcome.' They were met by a line of high-kicking drag queens and their now-legendary chant. The collective anger and solidarity was a turning point, igniting passionate debate about discrimination and forming the catalyst for the modern gay-rights movement — not just in New York but across the US and in countries from the Netherlands to Australia. On the one-year anniversary, the day was marked by the US's first LGBTIQ+ Pride march.

Conservatism was helped along by Senator Joseph 'Joe' McCarthy, who declared that homosexuals in the State Department threatened America's security and children. Tougher policing aimed to eradicate queer visibility in the public sphere, forcing the scene further underground in the 1940s and '50s. Yet on June 28, 1969, when police officers raided the Stonewall Inn – a gay-friendly watering hole in Greenwich Village – patrons did the unthinkable: they revolted. Fed up with both the harassment and corrupt officers receiving payoffs from the bars' owners (who were mostly organized-crime figures), they began bombarding the officers with coins, bottles, bricks and chants of 'gay power' and 'we shall overcome.' Their collective anger and solidarity was a turning point, igniting intense and passionate debate about discrimination and forming the catalyst for the modern gay-rights movement, not just in New York, but across the US and in countries from the Netherlands to Australia. On the one-year anniversary of the riots, the day was marked by the US's first LGBTIQ+ Pride march.

script_body: LGBTIQ+ activism intensified as AIDS hit headlines in the early 1980s. Writer Larry Kramer helped found ACT UP — the AIDS Coalition to Unleash Power — in 1987 to fight perceived homophobia and the price-gouging of AIDS drugs. One of its boldest protests came on September 14, 1989, when seven ACT UP protesters chained themselves to the VIP balcony of the New York Stock Exchange, demanding that Burroughs Wellcome lower the price of the AIDS drug AZT from a prohibitive $10,000 per patient per year. Within days, the price was slashed to $6400.

script_body: In 2013, New Yorkers reeled when Mark Carson, a Brooklyn man, was fatally shot in Greenwich Village — one of Manhattan's most historically tolerant neighborhoods. Carson and a friend had been walking along 8th St in the early hours of May 18 when, after a short altercation with a group of men hurling homophobic abuse, the 32-year-old was shot at point-blank range. The attack was a sobering reminder that even in liberal New York City, not everyone is happy to live and let live.

script_body: The heart of New York's local film scene was Queens' still-kicking Kaufman Astoria Studios. Founded by Jesse Lasky and Adolph Zukor in 1916 as a one-stop-shop for their Famous Players–Lasky Corporation, the complex produced a string of silent-era hits, among them The Sheik (1921) and Monsieur Beaucaire (1924), both starring Italian-born heartthrob Rudolph Valentino, as well as Manhandled (1924), starring early silver-screen diva Gloria Swanson. Renamed Paramount Pictures in 1927, the studios became known for turning Broadway stars into big-screen icons — among them the Marx Brothers, Fred Astaire, and Ginger Rogers, the latter making her feature-film debut as a flapper in Young Man of Manhattan (1930).

script_body: Despite Paramount moving all of its feature film shoots to Hollywood in 1932, the complex — renamed Eastern Services Studio — remained the home of Paramount's newsreel division. Throughout the 1930s it was also known for its 'shorts,' which launched the careers of homegrown talents including George Burns, Bob Hope, and Danny Kaye. After a stint making propaganda and training films for the US Army between WWII and 1970, the studios were renamed Kaufman Astoria Studios by George S. Kaufman — the real-estate magnate, not the playwright — in 1982. It was here that the Huxtables lived out their middle-class Brooklyn lives in the '80s TV sitcom The Cosby Show, and it's still here that small-screen favorite Sesame Street is taped.

After a stint making propaganda and training films for the US Army between WWII and 1970, what had become known as the US Signal Corps Photographic Center was renamed the Kaufman Astoria Studios by George S Kaufman (the real-estate magnate, not the playwright) in 1983. It was here that the Huxtables lived out their middle-class Brooklyn lives in the '80s TV sitcom The Cosby Show, where the heroine of Nurse Jackie juggled addictions and work, and the inmates of Litchfield Penitentiary battled their demons in Orange is the New Black. key_claims: Sex & the City (2008) jilting scene set at New York Public Library
Ghostbusters (1984) opening features NYPL marble lions and Rose Main Reading Room
NYPL foyer stands in for the Met in The Thomas Crown Affair (1999)
source_passage: Sarah Jessica Parker is less lucky in Sex & the City (2008), when a nervous Mr Big jilts her and her Vivienne Westwood wedding dress at the New York Public Library. Perhaps he'd seen Ghostbusters (1984) a few too many times, its opening scenes featuring the haunted library's iconic marble lions and Rose Main Reading Room. The library's foyer sneakily stands in for the Metropolitan Museum of Art in The Thomas Crown Affair (1999), in which thieving playboy Pierce Brosnan meets his match in sultry detective Rene Russo.

fact_check.omission_check: No omission. Marble lions (Patience & Fortitude) present; Rose Main Reading Room reopened after 2016 restoration. Ghostbusters, Thomas Crown Affair (lobby as the Met), and Sex and the City wedding all confirmed.

script_body: In Morningside Heights, Tom's Restaurant is the diner whose facade was used regularly in Seinfeld as the exterior of the fictional Monk's Diner.

physical_cues.cue: The blue-and-red exterior sign of Tom's Restaurant, the real-world Monk's Diner from Seinfeld

key_claims: Tom's Restaurant facade used regularly in Seinfeld
source_passage: The Upper West Side is also where you'll find Tom's Restaurant, the facade of which was used regularly in Seinfeld.

fact_check.omission_check: Tom's Restaurant (2880 Broadway at W 112th St) still open and operating as of 2026; exterior used as Monk's Cafe/Diner in Seinfeld confirmed. Neon sign (red/blue) intact. Neighborhood mislabeled.

corrections.original_text: On the Upper West Side, Tom's Restaurant
corrections.corrected_text: In Morningside Heights, Tom's Restaurant
corrections.reasoning: Tom's Restaurant is at 2880 Broadway / W 112th St in the Morningside Heights neighborhood (ground floor of Columbia's Armstrong Hall), not the Upper West Side. The UWS is generally bounded to the north around 110th St / Cathedral Pkwy; the diner sits a block above that. Multiple reputable sources (Wikipedia, Tripadvisor, The Infatuation) consistently label it Morningside Heights.

script_body: Lincoln Center is where Natalie Portman slowly loses her mind in the psychological thriller Black Swan (2010), and where love-struck Brooklynites Cher and Nicolas Cage meet for a date in Moonstruck (1987). The Center sits on what had previously been a rundown district of tenements, captured in Oscar-winning gangland musical West Side Story (1961) — the film was shot in those very streets just before they were demolished to build Lincoln Center.

physical_cues.cue: Lincoln Center plaza, setting of Black Swan and Moonstruck

key_claims: Black Swan (2010) filmed at Lincoln Center
Cher and Nicolas Cage meet at Lincoln Center in Moonstruck (1987)
West Side Story (1961) filmed in tenements on the site where Lincoln Center now stands
source_passage: Another neighborhood star is the elegant Lincoln Center, where Natalie Portman slowly loses her mind in the psychological thriller Black Swan (2010), and where love-struck Brooklynites Cher and Nicolas Cage meet for a date in Moonstruck (1987). The Center sits on what had previously been a rundown district of tenements, captured in Oscar-winning gangland musical West Side Story (1961).

fact_check.omission_check: Lincoln Center plaza/fountain intact. Black Swan (2010) filmed at Lincoln Center (Nina exits 66 St-Lincoln Center subway, enters on Columbus Ave); Moonstruck (1987) 'Meet me at the Met' scene at the Met Opera House/Lincoln Center fountain; West Side Story (1961) shot on West Side tenements (W 68th/Lincoln Square area) demolished for the Lincoln Center Urban Renewal project. All confirmed.

script_body: The Oscar-winner Birdman (2014) shines the spotlight on Midtown's glittering Theater District, in which a long-suffering Michael Keaton tries to stage a Broadway adaptation at the St James Theatre on W 44th St. Locked out of the building, a mortified Keaton fronts Times Square in nothing but his underwear. A few blocks further east, he spars over his play with Lindsay Duncan at historic drinking den Rum House.

physical_cues.cue: Times Square itself — the setting of the infamous underwear scene from Birdman

key_claims: Birdman (2014) filmed at St James Theatre on W 44th St
Michael Keaton's character appears in Times Square in underwear
Rum House bar used for confrontation scene
source_passage: The Oscar-winner Birdman (2014) shines the spotlight on Midtown's glittering Theater District, in which a long-suffering Michael Keaton tries to stage a Broadway adaptation at the St James Theatre on W44th St. Locked out of the building, a mortified Keaton fronts Times Square in nothing but his underwear. A few blocks further east, he spars over his play with Lindsay Duncan at historic drinking den Rum House.

fact_check.omission_check: Birdman (2014) used St James Theatre (W 44th St) and the Times Square underwear walk (shot after midnight); Rum House (Hotel Edison, W 47th St) used for the critic-bar scene with Lindsay Duncan as Tabitha Dickinson. All venues still operating. Times Square present. ('east' is the book's own framing.)

script_body: In the cult musical Fame (1980), New York High School of Performing Arts students do little for the city's traffic woes by dancing on Midtown's streets. The film's graphic content was too much for the city's Board of Education, who banned shooting at the real High School of Performing Arts, then located at 120 W 46th St. Consequently, filmmakers used the doorway of a disused church on the opposite side of the street for the school's entrance, and Haaren Hall (Tenth Ave and 59th St) for interior scenes.
key_claims: Fame (1980) students dance on Midtown streets
Board of Education banned filming at High School of Performing Arts at 120 W 46th St
A disused church across the street used for school entrance
Haaren Hall (Tenth Ave and 59th St) used for interiors
source_passage: Knives make way for leotards in the cult musical Fame (1980), in which New York High School of Performing Arts students do little for the city's traffic woes by dancing on Midtown's streets. The film's graphic content was too much for the city's Board of Education, who banned shooting at the real High School of Performing Arts, then located at 120 W 46th St. Consequently, filmmakers used the doorway of a disused church on the opposite side of the street for the school's entrance, and Haaren Hall (Tenth Ave and 59th St) for interior scenes.

fact_check.omission_check: Fame (1980): NYC Board of Education barred filming at the real High School of Performing Arts (120 W 46th St); a disused church across W 46th St used for the entrance; Haaren Hall (10th Ave & 59th St) used for interiors. All four claims confirmed. No physical cues in beat.

script_body: In On the Town (1949), starstruck sailors Frank Sinatra, Gene Kelly, and Jules Munshin skip, hop, and sing their way across the city from the base of Lady Liberty to Rockefeller Plaza and the Brooklyn Bridge. Another wave of campness hits the bridge when Diana Ross and Michael Jackson cross it in The Wiz (1978), a bizarre take on The Wizard of Oz, complete with munchkins in Flushing Meadows Corona Park and an Emerald City at the base of the WTC Twin Towers.

physical_cues.cue: Brooklyn Bridge — crossed by Frank Sinatra's sailors in On the Town and Diana Ross and Michael Jackson in The Wiz

key_claims: Brooklyn Bridge featured in On the Town (1949) with Sinatra, Kelly, Munshin
Brooklyn Bridge crossed by Diana Ross and Michael Jackson in The Wiz (1978)
The Wiz features munchkins in Flushing Meadows Corona Park and Emerald City at the base of the WTC Twin Towers
source_passage: In On the Town (1949), starstruck sailors Frank Sinatra, Gene Kelly and Jules Munshin look straight off a Pride float as they skip, hop and sing their way across this 'wonderful town,' from the base of Lady Liberty to Rockefeller Plaza and the Brooklyn Bridge. Another wave of campness hits the bridge when Diana Ross and Michael Jackson cross it in The Wiz (1978), a bizarre take on The Wizard of Oz, complete with munchkins in Flushing Meadows Corona Park and an Emerald City at the base of the WTC Twin Towers.

fact_check.omission_check: Brooklyn Bridge still standing and a working crossing; all film facts are historical and unchanged.
